activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: The stage manager records the blocking in the prompt book so that it can be repeated the same way at every performance.
story:
Coralie had agreed to direct the winter one-act because no one else wanted it, and now she stood in the empty auditorium with a pencil behind each ear, looking at a stage that seemed much larger than it had during assemblies. The play was a small strange thing about two siblings fighting over land beside a river, and she had liked it precisely because it problematized the idea of ownership, refusing to say who was right. That had seemed like a virtue when she read it alone. Now it seemed like a dare.

Angelo and Yuna arrived together, arguing about a chemistry test, and Mr. Kim unlocked the prop cabinet and left them to it, saying only that he would check in before five. Coralie cleared her throat in the way she had practiced and said they should start with the river scene. Angelo, who played the brother, asked what the river was. She pointed at the third row of seats. "It's out there," she said. "It floods the whole riparian zone by the end. You have to keep stepping back from it."

They ran it three times and it was terrible each time in a new way. Angelo crossed to the left when the argument rose; Yuna, playing the sister, crossed to the right; they ended up facing each other from opposite wings like people on two separate stages. Coralie tried describing the scene's causality to them, how the brother's insult had to come before the sister's retreat or the retreat meant nothing, and Angelo said, not unkindly, "I can't track the psychology every single time. Tell me where to walk."

She thought about that on the bus home. Part of her wanted the movements to grow out of feeling, discovered fresh at every performance, and part of her had begun to suspect that the feeling would only ever come if the walking was settled first. She did not know yet how to hold both of those at once. The next afternoon she brought a bound notebook with grid pages and a sharpened pencil, and before they started she asked Yuna to sit at the table by the wing with it.

"Stage managers write it all down," Coralie said. "The blocking, every cross, every turn. It goes in the prompt book."

"So it can be the same every show," Yuna said, already ruling a small stage diagram onto the first page.

"So it can be the same every show," Coralie repeated, and something in her resisted it even as she said it, the same way she resisted the tidy ending of a poem. But she had a page of her own now, covered in arrows, and when she told Angelo to cross downstage right on his line about the fence, he did it, and Yuna's retreat landed a beat later, and for four lines the scene breathed.

They rehearsed for eleven days. Mr. Kim watched twice and suggested she give the river scene more air, and she took the note, mostly. She still changed small things when a run felt dead, and each time she called out the change to Yuna, who wrote it in without complaint. By dress rehearsal the notebook was fat with taped-in pages, and Coralie had stopped apologizing for the arrows.

On opening night the house was small and attentive, and the scene was going well until it wasn't. Angelo, rattled by a dropped prop in the previous scene, took his cross early, moving left while Yuna was still speaking, and she faltered, and in the wings afterward, between acts, they stood in the dark with their voices low and sharp. "I moved when I was supposed to," Angelo said. "You never moved, that's why I went." Yuna said, "That is not what happened."

Coralie felt the argument assembling itself like weather. She wanted to say she trusted them both, but trust was not a fact. Yuna was already flipping through the notebook, flashlight under her chin, and she turned it toward them, open to the river scene, the little ruled stage with its arrows, Coralie's own handwriting showing the brother's cross written after the sister's line, not before. They looked at it for a long moment. "Okay," Angelo said. "After."

They went back out for the second act, and the crossing came in its right place, and the brother stepped back from the river that only the audience could see, and Coralie stood in the dark by the prompt book watching the movement she had chosen happen again exactly as recorded. She did not know whether it was better because it was repeated or only safer. Yuna turned a page and wrote something new in the margin, and the pencil scratched, and downstage the lights were going to blue.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In a 2014 study led by David Yeager, students were more likely to revise essays when critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them.
story:
Jade had been chosen to give the defensive feedback, which meant she had to stand in front of Myles after the last scrimmage and tell him, in front of nobody but with the whole gym listening, that his closeouts were late. It was the third week of the season and the coach had instituted peer review, an idea he had borrowed, he said, from his education courses, and which he was trying to codify into a set of rules taped to the door: Be specific. Be kind. Be honest. The rules were in that order, and Jade suspected the order mattered, though she could not have said how.

The problem was that she had done this before, badly. Freshman year, in the library during a group project, she had told Colten that his half of the presentation was obvious and rushed, which was true, and which he had received by closing his laptop and not speaking to her for a month. She had spent that month arguing, silently, that honesty was the higher virtue. She had spent the two years since noticing how his shoulders dropped whenever she started a sentence, and wondering whether her honesty had been a principle or just a habit of noticing flaws and letting them out.

Practice ended with ten minutes of free throws, and Myles, predictably, missed his first four. He was the best athlete on a moribund team, two wins from last season, a boy who could get his hand above the rim and yet let his man blow by him on the perimeter again and again because he was slow to recover when he helped inside. The gym smelled like rubber and cold air. The coach had left early, some family thing, which meant the feedback was unsupervised, which meant it would count for something or nothing, depending entirely on Jade.

She thought about her psychology elective, which she had taken only because the lab science sections were full. In November Ms. Popal had spent fifteen minutes on feedback, and most of it had slid off Jade, but one thing had stuck. She had even written it in the margin of her notebook, where she wrote things she did not understand yet. "In 2014," she said to Colten once, on the bus, testing it out, "David Yeager led a study where students were more likely to revise their essays when the critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them." Colten had said that sounded like a trick, like wrapping a pill in cheese for a dog. Jade had said maybe, but the dog took the pill.

She called Myles over near the water bottles. He came with his chin already set, the look of somebody bracing for the word "but." She recognized the look because she had seen it on Colten's face in the library, and she had called it thin skin then, and she was less sure now. Maybe it was just a person deciding, in the half second before you spoke, whether you were for him or against him, and there was nothing thin about the calculation.

"Myles," she said. "I think you're the best player on this team, and I think you can be the best defender in the league. That's why I want to tell you this." His eyebrows moved, a small recalibration. She kept going before she could soften it. "Your closeouts are late. It happened six times in the scrimmage. You help on the drive, and then you float back instead of sprinting, and your man shoots. That's the whole thing. If you sprint the recovery, nobody scores on us from the wing."

He turned the water bottle in his hands. She waited, and the wait was worse than the saying, because in the wait she could hear every way it might go wrong. Then he said, "Six times?" and she said, "I counted," and he said, "Show me one," and they walked to the wing, and she played the guard, driving, while he helped off her imaginary man and floated back, and she stopped him and said, "There. You're jogging. You have to sprint," and he did it again, and this time he arrived with his hand up and his feet set, and he said, "Like that?" and she said, "Like that."

Later, on the bench, lacing her shoes, she thought about what she had actually done. She had not lied. She had led with the belief because a study said it worked, and that felt closer to manipulation than she wanted it to, a technique learned from a margin note and deployed on a teammate. But she had also meant it, both parts, the belief and the criticism, and she could not find the line between using a thing and knowing it. Colten, gathering cones across the gym, called over and asked how the feedback had gone, and Jade said it went okay, and he said, "You didn't make him quit, that's new," and she laughed, and then Myles, from the doorway with his bag on his shoulder, called back into the gym, "Same time tomorrow, right? Count my closeouts again."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Progressive overload means gradually increasing training demands, such as weight, distance or intensity, so the body keeps having a reason to adapt.
story:
Sienna had been running the same loop for four months, and for three of those months her times had refused to budge. She knew this because she kept a spreadsheet, color-coded, which her mother called obsessive and which Sienna preferred to call rigorous. On the first Saturday of June she carried the spreadsheet, a folding chair, and a glass of lemonade into the backyard, spread the papers across the picnic table, and prepared to confront the evidence.

The evidence was not encouraging. Her loop was 5K, run every single morning before school, at more or less the same pace, on more or less the same legs. The numbers stared back at her from the page in their tidy cells, and something about their tidiness began to strike her as suspicious. She was working hard. She was not improving. These two facts sat next to each other on the table like guests who refused to speak.

Ella arrived first, barefoot across the grass, holding a popsicle she was eating with the urgency of someone who had bought it from a truck minutes ago. "You look like a detective," she said, nodding at the papers. "Who died?"

"Nothing died. That's the problem. Nothing is happening at all."

Hamzah came through the side gate a few minutes later with his phone in his hand, which was how Hamzah traveled everywhere, like a man carrying his own weather. He leaned over the table, scrolled through Sienna's times, and did his annoying low whistle. "You've done the exact same workout for months," he said. "Of course it stopped working."

"Why of course?"

"Because the body only changes if you keep giving it a reason to." He turned the phone toward her. His cousin ran track at a college two states away, and Hamzah had spent an entire bus ride home from a meet interrogating him about it. "He kept saying this phrase. Progressive overload. It means gradually increasing the training demands, like the distance or the intensity or whatever, so your body keeps having a reason to adapt."

Sienna read the screen, then looked at her own spreadsheet, and felt the small vertigo of a locked door turning out never to have been locked. Her embryonic plan, sketched that morning in pencil, suddenly needed more than penciling. She needed a structure, not a ritual. She needed, she realized, to think less like someone proving her devotion through repetition and more like someone building something week by week.

"Also," Hamzah added, with the mild cruelty of a friend, "you never warm up. My cousin says you're supposed to warm up. And rest. Actual rest days. Days where you do nothing."

"Nothing?"

"Nothing. Watch television. Contemplate your spreadsheet from the couch."

Ella laughed so hard the popsicle stick fell into the grass, and Sienna could not entirely exculpate herself from the charge, because there was a tab in her spreadsheet labeled REST?, containing only a question mark and, for reasons she could no longer defend, a small footnote. She turned to a clean sheet of paper and began building the week in earnest. Monday, easy run and a warm-up that was not just standing around deciding to run. Tuesday, the loop, but longer. Wednesday, nothing. She wrote NOTHING in capitals, then crossed it out and wrote it again, smaller, as if to reassure herself that rest at a reasonable size still counted.

The afternoon light moved across the table while she worked, and the shadow of the fence posts shifted like a slow clock. When she hesitated over Thursday, unsure whether to push the distance or the pace, she did not pretend to know. She circled both, drew an arrow between them, and let the arrow sit there, undecided. Mr. Jung, the neighbor, leaned over the fence to water his tomatoes, and she asked him, half-joking, whether a person could do both in one week. He considered the question longer than she expected, then said only that his tomatoes had taught him the same lesson every year: too much water and they sulked, too little and they sulked, and the right amount changed with the weather. Sienna thanked him, and Ella asked if the tomatoes also did progressive overload, and Mr. Jung said, without looking up, that he was not going to discuss the morphology of his garden with teenagers who dropped popsicle sticks in his grass.

Ella retrieved the stick with great ceremony. Hamzah flipped the spreadsheet to its final page and said the plan looked like an actual plan now, embryonic but real, and Sienna folded the paper along its fresh creases and put it in the pocket of her shorts. "Tomorrow I warm up first," she said. "And Thursday we'll see." Then she picked up the folding chair, shook the grass off the legs, and carried it toward the garage with the chair balanced on her hip and the plan tapping against her thigh at every step.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: At the top of its path a projectile's vertical velocity is zero, but its horizontal velocity is not, so it is still moving.
story:
The skate park had emptied by six, except for the bowl's deep end where Mavrick was still trying the same gap he'd failed all summer. Charlotte sat on the coping with her physics notebook open on her knees, because Ms. Ivanova had announced a test Monday and Charlotte had decided, against all her habits, to study somewhere with witnesses. Kylie lay on the flat concrete beside her, phone held above her face, editing the video she'd taken of Mavrick's last attempt.

"He almost had it that time," Kylie said, without looking up.

"He didn't almost have it. He almost died." Charlotte turned a page. The problem she was stuck on involved a ball launched at an angle, and the textbook wanted her to split the velocity into horizontal and vertical parts, as if one motion could be two motions at once, which felt like a lie she was being asked to sign.

Mavrick climbed out of the bowl, breathing hard, and dropped onto the concrete. "Show me the last one."

Kylie scrubbed the video backward. On the screen, Mavrick's board left the coping and rose in a clean arc, and Kylie's thumb slowed it down so the whole flight unspooled at a crawl. The board hung near the top of its curve, and Mavrick leaned toward the screen like an acolyte studying a relic.

"See," he said. "Right there. It stops. For a second it's just, like, stopped in the air."

"It's not stopped," Charlotte said, and then heard herself, and didn't know why she was sure.

"It looks stopped."

Charlotte took the phone from Kylie and ran the slow motion back to the top of the arc, watching the board slide sideways across the frame, frame by frame, unmistakably traveling. "Look at where it is against the fence. It's moving the whole time. At the top the vertical velocity is zero, but the horizontal isn't. It's still moving."

"That's one frame," Mavrick said.

"It's every frame." She ran it again. "It never stops. It just stops going up."

Mavrick took the phone and watched it twice more, and his face went through something complicated, the way it did when he lost an argument he'd enjoyed having. "Okay," he said finally. "Okay, that's actually cool."

What was strange was that Charlotte hadn't known that a moment before. She'd read the chapter twice, she'd copied the diagram, and only now, with the board drifting sideways through Kylie's cheap slow motion, did the two halves of the motion come apart in her head and refuse to rejoin into a single simple thing. She looked down at her problem set. The ball at the top of its arc. Vertical velocity zero, horizontal velocity whatever it had been at launch, unchanged, carrying on. She penciled in the first line of the solution and it was right, she could feel it was right, though she could not have said how she knew.

"Text me if you get the rest," Kylie said, standing, brushing off her jeans. "I'm going to cajole my brother into driving us food."

"Tell him I'll owe him."

"He doesn't want your money. He wants you to tell Mom he drove responsibly last weekend."

"That's blackmail."

"That's negotiation." Kylie pocketed her phone and walked off across the parking lot, and her shadow stretched thin and long in front of her, moving faster than she was.

Mavrick stayed. He watched Charlotte work for a while, then said, "Do the thing with the board again." She showed him, the arc, the top, the sideways slide. He nodded slowly. "So when I'm up there," he said, "I'm never actually still."

"You're never actually still," Charlotte said.

He sat with that for a moment, turning his board over in his hands. Then he stood, rolled to the edge of the coping, and set his feet. Charlotte watched him drop into the bowl and pump toward the gap, and as he rose off the lip she caught herself watching for it, the top of the arc, the instant his vertical velocity hit zero, and the fact that he kept moving sideways the whole time, that his body crossed the sky even at the very peak of his leaving it.

He landed it. He rolled away whooping, one hand flung up, and Charlotte laughed and clapped the notebook shut.

Monday, Ms. Ivanova read the test problems aloud while she set out the papers, and the second one began, "A ball is thrown at an angle." Charlotte's pencil was already moving, splitting the velocity in two, when she heard Mavrick mutter behind her, to nobody, "It's still moving," and she had to press her lips together to keep the smile off her face while she wrote.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Sabbath commandment appears twice in the Hebrew Bible with different reasons: Exodus 20 cites God resting after creation, while Deuteronomy 5 cites Israel's release from slavery in Egypt.
story:
The debate was in six days, and James had chosen the one question the rabbi's study group had warned would split the room in half: whether the commandment to keep the Sabbath still bound anyone in a world of Sunday shifts and Saturday tournaments. He sat at the long table in the synagogue library with two Bibles open in front of him, one turned to Exodus, one to Deuteronomy, and a legal pad filling with arrows that connected nothing yet.

Kieran arrived late, shaking rain off his jacket, and slid into the chair across from James without asking what the arrows meant. He had a habit of reading upside down. "You've written 'why' four times on this page," he said.

"Because the text doesn't say the same thing twice." James turned the Exodus Bible around and put his finger under the line. The Sabbath commandment appeared in both books, the words almost identical, and that near-identity was the problem. "In Exodus it says God rested after creation, so the day belongs to God. In Deuteronomy it says something else entirely. It says remember that you were slaves in Egypt and were set free, so the day belongs to the people who were freed."

Kieran read both passages twice, lips moving slightly, the way he did with anything he planned to argue against. "So which one is it?"

"That's the debate, apparently." James had assumed there was one answer, the way a law has one wording, and had spent three evenings looking for the authoritative version only to find there wasn't one. There was only the argument between the two.

Mr. Mensah, who ran the study group and taught history at the high school, came through the doorway carrying a tray with three cups of tea, because he had a way of knowing when people had skipped dinner. He set one within James's reach and one within Kieran's and sat down at the end of the table without looking at the notes. He had told them at the start of the term that he would not tell them what the text meant; his job, he said, was to make sure they read slowly enough to notice when it changed its mind.

The third cup sat untouched, and James pushed it toward the door a minute before Arnaud came in, hair still wet from the walk. Arnaud's mother worked nights at the hospital, and he had once told James that Saturday was the only day she slept past six, which was why he kept showing up to these debates at all. He wrapped both hands around the cup and said, "Tell me what I missed."

James had been thinking about Arnaud's mother all week without realizing it. In the summer, before the group had ever met, there had been an afternoon at his grandfather's kitchen table, a memory that surfaced now with the smell of the tea. His grandfather had two enormous books and read the commandment aloud from each one, and when James asked why the reasons differed, his grandfather only smiled and said, "You ask that every year." His cousins had been there, one quoting Exodus and one quoting Deuteronomy, each insisting the other had it wrong, and his grandfather had refused to adjudicate, letting them argue until the challah was gone. James had thought at the time that the old man simply enjoyed the noise.

Now he understood it differently, though not completely, and he said as much. "Here's my position, and I'm not sure how much of it I can defend. If you read Exodus, the Sabbath is about creation, about the rhythm being built into the world, and that applies to everyone. If you read Deuteronomy, it's about a specific people who were enslaved and then freed, and the day exists so they never forget what rest is worth. Those aren't the same rule. One says the day is sacred because God stopped. The other says it's sacred because you were once not allowed to stop."

"Which one do you argue?" Arnaud asked.

"Both, against each other. If I only use one, someone in the audience holds up the other book and I lose." He looked at the two open Bibles, the arrows abandoned. "The honest version is that the text itself disagrees, or at least doesn't settle it, and maybe a rule that gets repeated with two different reasons is a rule that expects you to keep asking."

Kieran leaned back. "That's not a position. That's a shrug."

"It's a position with a shrug attached," James said. "I can argue that a law about rest for the overworked has more to say now than a law about imitating the creator, or I can argue the opposite, and part of my honesty is admitting I don't know which the text prefers. I only know it gives me both doors."

Mr. Mensah wrote something on his own pad, folded the page once, and slid it down the table. James opened it and found a single line, not a verdict but a question: which reason would you give to someone who has never been free? He read it twice, then looked up at Arnaud, who was turning his empty cup in slow circles, and at Kieran, who had already pulled Deuteronomy toward himself and begun to read aloud, one finger under each line, testing the words like a floor before stepping out onto it.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: On level ground with no air resistance, a launch angle of 45 degrees gives the greatest range for a given launch speed.
story:
The garage smelled of cut pine and motor oil, and the ball launcher stood on the workbench like something halfway between a toy and a weapon. Gavin had built it from a leaf spring and two door hinges, and for three weekends it had thrown tennis balls into the neighbor's yard at angles nobody had chosen on purpose. Tomorrow was the distance contest at the science fair. Tonight they had to decide the angle.

Stephen wanted sixty degrees. He kept pointing at the sky, saying the ball needed room to fly, and Juliet kept looking at the tape measure she had laid across the driveway like a runway. "Sixty looks impressive," she said. "Impressive doesn't win. Distance wins." Stephen called her an iconoclast, pleased with the word, and she said thank you.

They had a book open on the hood of the car, chapter eleven, projectile motion. Gavin read it twice and the second time something loosened in his head. The trick, he told them, was to stop thinking of the throw as one thing. You split the velocity into a horizontal piece and a vertical piece. The horizontal piece never changes; the vertical piece fights gravity the whole way up and back down. "So the angle is you deciding how to spend a fixed budget," he said. "Steep buys you airtime. Flat buys you speed along the ground."

Stephen said that was the most boring description of throwing anything, ever, and Gavin admitted it might be. Juliet pulled out her phone and started typing numbers. She was quiet for a minute, then she looked up. "The book says forty-five degrees," she said. "On level ground, no air resistance, forty-five gives the greatest range for a given launch speed."

Gavin didn't believe it right away. It felt like a rumor. But the contest launcher would sit on the gym floor, which was level, and the ball was small enough that air resistance seemed like a problem for a windier day, and the spring would shove with the same strength no matter where they aimed it. Given launch speed. That part mattered. He adjusted the protractor mount to forty-five, cranked the arm back, and Juliet marked his hand position on the spring with chalk so they would launch identically every time.

The first ball went farther than any ball had gone all month. It cleared the driveway, cleared the sidewalk, and incapacitated a garbage can at the curb, which toppled over with a sound like a filing cabinet falling downstairs. Stephen laughed so hard he had to sit down on the mower. "Our science fair project is a weapon," he said. "I take back everything."

They ran it twenty more times while the light died, Juliet calling the angles from a little table she had made, thirty-five, forty, forty-five, fifty, sixty, chalk marking where each ball first touched ground. The forty-five throws won more often than not, though not every time, and that bothered Gavin more than he expected. He stood at the tape measure with his hands in his pockets. "The book says forty-five is best," he said. "Our data mostly agrees. Mostly isn't exactly." Juliet said the wind changed, the chalk marks were fuzzy, and Stephen's cranking was never twice the same. "Or the book is wrong," Stephen offered, hopeful.

Ms. Ngo from next door came out to retrieve her garbage can from the gutter, and she looked at the launcher, the tape measure, the scatter of tennis balls across her lawn. She asked what they were doing, and Gavin explained the contest and the angle and the split velocities, gesturing with his hands like the arc itself. She listened all the way through, which few adults did, and then she said, "So which angle are you going with?" Gavin told her forty-five, and that they had measured it, and that he still wasn't sure whether the misses were the world's fault or theirs. She said that was the correct way to be unsure.

When she had carried the can back up her drive, they packed the launcher into the wagon. Juliet folded the tape measure into a neat square and handed Gavin the chalk, their putative lucky charm now, white and worn to a stub. Stephen wheeled the wagon toward the garage door and stopped.

"Bet you a milkshake the can goes over again tomorrow."

"You're on," Gavin said, and clicked the spring lock shut.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something that a character on stage does not, which lets a short scene build tension quickly.
story:
Kaylee had qualified for the state tournament in Lincoln-Douglas debate, which was the problem, because the state tournament now also ran a one-act playwriting event, and Ms. McKenzie had signed her up for both without asking. "You have three weeks," Ms. McKenzie said, handing her a flyer in the band room. "A ten-minute play about a moment from your own life. It gets staged Saturday morning, between your rounds. Bring the script typed."

She wrote the first draft in the cafeteria with her debate partner, Chayce, who was reading evidence cards about school lunch policy. "What's your play about?" he asked.

"Thanksgiving at my grandmother's, two years ago. She'd gotten a letter saying her annuity payments were stopping, the one she'd paid into for thirty years, and she hid it under the fruit bowl and cooked the whole dinner anyway. Nobody found out until January."

"That's good material," Chayce said. "Very depressing. Judges love that."

The draft was four pages of people passing green bean casserole and saying nothing. She read it aloud in the empty debate room and it lay there like a dropped napkin. Nothing happened. The audience, if there ever was one, would sit through seven minutes of small talk waiting for a letter they didn't know existed.

At the tournament on Friday, between preliminary rounds, she found Mark from her econ class eating fries in the hallway outside the gym. Mark had done the playwriting event last year and placed third with a piece about his brother's appendix. "Show me the script," he said, and she watched him read it, which was worse than just being told it was bad. He tapped page two. "Here. This is where you lose everybody. The grandmother knows about the letter and we don't, so we're just watching a family be quiet."

"So make her tell them sooner?"

"No, keep it hidden. Let us see it first. Like, she takes the letter out and reads it alone before anyone arrives, and the audience watches her put it under the fruit bowl. Then the family walks in and starts complimenting the turkey, and we're all sitting there screaming internally." He pointed at her. "Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something that a character on stage does not. That's the whole engine. You get it in one short scene and the tension builds by itself."

"Is that a rule?"

"It's a fact of the universe," Mark said, and stole one of her fries.

She rewrote the first two pages that night in the hotel business center, next to a printer jam and a vending machine that hummed like a wasp. The play opened with the grandmother alone at the table, holding the letter, reading it twice, folding it into quarters and sliding it under the fruit bowl between a banana and two pears. Then the doorbell, and Kaylee's own stage directions brought in the family, including a teenage girl based on Kaylee who complained about the cranberry sauce being from a can.

Saturday morning they staged it in a classroom with the desks pushed against the wall. Ms. McKenzie had roped in two students from another school to read the aunt and the uncle, and Kaylee read the grandmother and herself, switching voices, which got a laugh when the teenage girl and the grandmother argued. The letter sat under the plastic fruit the whole time. Every time an aunt reached for a pear, three people in the front row leaned forward. A kid in a Debate Is My Cardio shirt whispered "don't move the pears" and had to be shushed by his own coach.

The judge's ballot came back with one word circled twice at the top, perspicacious, which Kaylee had to look up on her phone, and with a comment that said the fruit bowl was doing more work than most full-length plays she'd judged. Under weaknesses it said the teenage girl needed more than sass, and Kaylee thought that was fair, since the girl was her, and she had not figured out yet whether she'd been a coward or just thirteen at the time.

She broke to semifinals in debate and lost on a 2-1 decision about whether school lunch programs stigmatize the students who use them, which felt, sitting in the hallway afterward with her flowsheet, like a question she'd been circling all weekend from another direction. The playwriting results were posted by the gym doors on a single sheet of paper. She was second. The first-place play was about a boy and his appendix. Mark found her at the sheet, read it, and said, "You lost to my appendix. I'd be furious."

"I'm not," she said, and found it was mostly true, except for the part of her that was already rewriting the teenage girl, giving her one moment alone with the fruit bowl before the doorbell rang, a moment where she almost lifted it and set it back down. She said goodbye to the pear she'd borrowed for rehearsal, handed it back to the girl from the other school, and went to find Chayce for the bus.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Hanukkah menorah has nine branches: eight for the nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others, one more each night.
story:
The apartment smelled of fried latkes and cardamom, and Alex stood in the kitchen doorway holding the box of candles his grandmother had pressed into his hands, feeling the weight of being eighteen and trusted. It was the fourth night of Hanukkah, and for the first year since he could remember, his grandfather was not the one who would light the menorah. Grandpa had died in March, quietly, between a cardiologist appointment and a Sunday crossword, and the family had gathered tonight at Aunt Rina's partly to prove that they still could.

"Four candles tonight," his mother said from the stove, not turning around. "Plus the shamash." She said it lightly, the way you remind someone of something they already know, and Alex nodded and took the menorah down from the shelf above the refrigerator, the old brass one with its arms darkened by decades of flame. He rubbed a cloth over the stem without thinking, a habit that used to be his grandfather's, and the metal came up dull gold where he burnished it.

He laid the candles out on the counter and began to set them, and somewhere between his cousin shrieking over a gift and his uncle arriving late and loud, he lost the thread of his own count. He stared at the menorah's nine branches and could not remember whether he had placed three of the night's candles or four, and whether the tall one in the middle, the one his grandfather always lit first, counted. His stomach dropped in a way that felt disproportionate, and he understood that it wasn't really about candles.

He texted Murray, who had sat next to him in world history and once argued with the teacher for a full period about whether tradition was knowledge or just inertia. Murray replied fast: "look it up, that's what you'd tell me." Alex grinned despite himself, then found Savanna's name instead, because Savanna was the one who actually celebrated things. She answered with a single line: "Eight for the nights, plus the shamash, the helper candle that lights the others. One more each night." Then a second message: "you're lighting it??? that's huge."

So he counted again, slowly, touching each branch. Eight for the nights, and the ninth held the helper, which his grandfather had called the shamash with a shrug, as if the candle were an old friend. Alex put that one in last, in its own branch, and understood that the count he'd botched was four, because the helper stood apart and didn't belong to the nights at all. The relief was physical, a loosening in his shoulders, though he noticed it came mixed with something less tidy, a suspicion that he was performing grief correctly rather than simply feeling it.

Aunt Rina's table was an epicurean ruin by the time they gathered around the menorah: platters of latkes gone cold at the edges, sour cream, a tin of the butter cookies his grandfather used to hoard. His grandmother took her seat nearest the window, and the room quieted in a way that gathered everyone without anyone asking for it. Alex struck the match. His hand was steadier than he expected, and he lit the shamash first, then the four, right to left as his grandfather had done, murmuring the blessings in the half-remembered Hebrew that came out more like his grandfather's voice than his own.

Afterward his cousins dispersed toward dessert and his uncles toward argument, but his grandmother stayed in her chair, watching the small flames lean together. "He would have made some joke about you counting on your fingers," she said. Alex laughed, and then didn't, because the laugh had nowhere to go. He sat down on the floor beside her chair, which is where he had sat at seven, and the candles made a soft consonance of light against the dark window, five flames where the family had expected exactly that number, and none where the man who usually struck the match should have been standing.

He could not decide, sitting there, whether he believed the candles meant anything beyond themselves, whether his grandfather was anywhere the light reached, and he let both possibilities sit side by side without forcing them to agree. His grandmother reached down and straightened the collar of his shirt the way she had done at every holiday of his childhood. "Same time tomorrow," she said. "Fifth night. Five candles." Alex looked up at the menorah and counted the empty branches that remained, and said, "Plus the shamash."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: DNA copying is semiconservative: each new double helix keeps one strand from the original molecule and pairs it with one newly built strand.
story:
The community garden behind the rec center had eleven plots and a plastic bin of tools that nobody locked, and Jordyn had claimed the corner plot with the worst soil because Ms. Li had said the fail rate on the plot was the lowest rent. She was there on a Saturday morning in June with a biology textbook open on an overturned bucket, because she had failed the unit test on DNA and had one week to pass a retest or lose her spot in the fall microbiology course.

Emma and Aidan came through the chain-link gate at ten, arguing before they were all the way through it. Emma was carrying a bag of seedlings and Aidan was carrying nothing, which was usual. They had both passed the test, and Jordyn had asked them to come quiz her, mostly because Emma owed her for covering a shift at the pool and Aidan would come anywhere Emma went.

"It's all new," Aidan said, dropping onto the grass beside the bucket. "That's the whole point of copying. You copy a document, the copy is a copy. New."

"You're wrong," Emma said. "It's half old. Every single time."

Jordyn picked a slug off a seedling and flicked it into the weeds. She had read the chapter twice last night and the word they were circling had not stuck. She knew about transcription, how the code got read off into a working copy, and translation, how that working copy got read into a chain of amino acids, and she could recite both processes on the walk from the bus stop. But the copying itself, the part before all that, had stayed a blur.

"Half old how," she said.

"That's the thing," Emma said, sitting down. "When a DNA molecule gets copied, you end up with two molecules. Each one is a double helix. And each one keeps one strand from the original molecule, the actual physical strand, and pairs it with one strand that's newly built."

Aidan pulled a grass blade apart lengthwise, the way he did when he was losing. "So one molecule is all old and one is all new."

"No. Both of them are half and half. One old strand, one new strand, in each."

"There's a word for it," Aidan said. "It was on the test."

"Semiconservative," Emma said. Jordyn wrote it on her wrist with a pen because her notebook was across the plot, and the word sat there in Emma's looping recitation of the definition, which Jordyn made her give twice more, word for word, until it was fixed.

They spent the next hour weeding and quizzing, and the quizzing was where the trouble started, because Jordyn kept collapsing the two halves of the unit into one. She would describe transcription and slide straight into amino acids without marking the boundary. Emma corrected her each time, gently, and Aidan corrected her loudly, and Jordyn felt the two processes grinding against each other in her head the way the tectonic plates were supposed to grind under the science museum's floor, the exhibit with the lit-up diagram they had all stood on in eighth grade. Transcription made the working copy. Translation read that copy into protein. Two steps, and she was trying to make them one, and it kept failing.

Ms. Li came by at noon with her watering can and stood at the fence a while, listening, before she asked what they were studying. Jordyn told her, bracing for a lecture, but Ms. Li only said, "Explain it to the beans, then. They're doing it right now in every cell. If you can tell the plants how they manage it, you know it." Then she walked on to the tomato cages, which was her way of not hovering.

Jordyn stood over the bean row. She crouched and put her hand flat on a leaf, which felt cooler than the air, and started talking in a low voice, and this was the heuristic that worked: talk to something that cannot interrupt. Transcription first, the code being read off into the working copy inside the nucleus. Then the copy going out. Then translation, the reading of it into amino acids, the chain folding up into the protein that made the leaf, the bean, the climb up the string. And underneath all of it, before any of it could happen, the copying, semiconservative, each new double helix keeping one strand from the original molecule and pairing it with one newly built strand, so that the cell's inheritance was never fully new and never fully old. She said it to the beans twice and heard, the second time, that she had gotten it whole.

"Are you actually talking to those," Aidan said from the grass.

"It worked, didn't it," Jordyn said. "You should try talking to something that can't walk away from you."

Emma laughed, and then came the twist, because Emma leaned over the textbook to check one of the practice questions and said, slowly, that she had written the wrong molecule in her answer on the original test. She had described the working copy as DNA. The marker had taken two points off and she had passed anyway, 51 out of 60, and she had never gone back to look at what she got wrong. She sat with the pen between her fingers. "I've been telling you the boundaries all morning like I own them."

"You got the semiconservative part right," Jordyn said. "The copying part. Word for word."

"That's the part I'm sure of," Emma said. "The part in between is where I fell through."

Aidan pulled the grass blade apart all the way down to the root and held up the two halves. Jordyn took one from him, folded it in half, and put it in the book as a page marker at the transcription chapter. "Quiz me again tomorrow," she said. "Start with the part none of us is sure of."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: In mayonnaise, lecithin and proteins from egg yolk act as emulsifiers, holding tiny oil droplets suspended in water so the sauce does not separate.
story:
Lucas had promised his grandmother a proper dinner before she came home from her Thursday appointment, and by five o'clock the kitchen smelled of roast chicken and thyme, which so far was the only thing going according to plan. The plan had holes in it. The plan, for instance, had not accounted for the potato salad requiring mayonnaise, or for the jar in the fridge holding approximately one teaspoon of the stuff, or for his grandmother's handwritten recipe book opening to a page that said, in her looping script, "Make it yourself. It's only eggs and oil and patience, and you have two of those."

He called Umar first, because Umar answered on the first ring and Hamza answered on the fourth, which told you most of what you needed to know about them. "You're making mayo from scratch," Umar said, in the tone he used for people who claimed they could juggle. "Whisk the oil in slowly. Slowly. My mum says everyone pours too fast and it splits."

"It's not going to split," Lucas said, holding his phone between ear and shoulder while he cracked an egg and separated the yolk into his grandmother's yellow mixing bowl, the one with a chip shaped like a shark bite. He added a spoonful of mustard, a squeeze of lemon, and began whisking. Then he began pouring. The oil went in, the whisk went round, and for one shining moment the whole thing looked like mayonnaise, thick and pale and glossy, and Lucas felt the particular pride of a man who has defeated a recipe.

Then it turned to soup. Not even good soup. A yellowish liquid with a slick of oil floating on top, pooling in the bowl's shark bite like a small malicious lake. He whisked harder, which did nothing, and then he whisked violently, which also did nothing, and then he took a photo and sent it to the group chat with the caption "science has failed us."

Hamza replied within seconds: "that's not mayo that's the La Brea tar pits." Umar sent a single crying face. Lucas stared at the bowl and felt something in his chest that a sandwich would not assuage. In the recipe book, between his grandmother's notes, someone had pencilled in the margin years ago: "If it breaks, ask Grandad." Which suggested that this had happened before, to someone, and that it had not been the end of the world.

His grandfather was in the garden taking apart a bird feeder, which was his version of meditation. He came in when called, washed his hands without being asked, looked into the bowl for a long moment, and said, "Ah. The lake." He cracked a fresh egg, separated the yolk into a clean bowl with the speed of a man who had done it ten thousand times, and whisked a spoonful of the failed liquid into it, drop by drop, then more, then all of it, and the whole broken mess drew together into something thick and gold and alive-looking. He tapped the bowl. "Emulsifiers," he said, as if introducing an old friend. "The yolk's full of them."

Lucas took over the whisking, because it was his dinner and also because his grandfather had a way of hovering that suggested hovering was the actual hobby. While he whisked he looked things up on his phone, one-handed, and found that in mayonnaise the lecithin and the proteins from egg yolk hold tiny oil droplets suspended in water so the sauce does not separate, which explained the lake the way a map explains a country you've already walked across. He read a fragment aloud. His grandfather grunted approval and said that in his day you had to trust the yolk on faith. Lucas said that was probably why everything took so long back then, and his grandfather said, with great dignity, that everything taking longer had been the entire point.

While the chicken rested, Mr. Nwosu from next door appeared at the fence and stayed for the mayonnaise debate, which had somehow become about whether carbon was the true kitchen element, since it made both the sugar and the burnt pan. "Diamond and graphite, same atom, different allotrope," he said, gesturing at the charcoal of a previous, less successful attempt still soaking in the sink. "Like you," he told Lucas. "Same boy before and after dinner, entirely different person depending on whether he's been fed." Hamza, who had arrived on foot because he claimed the photo of the tar pits had moved him, stole a spoon of the rescued mayo, tasted it, and took a moment of silence. "Okay," he said. "Okay. This is unfair to Hellmann's."

They ate on the back step because it was warm, and the potato salad was the first thing to go, and the evening light on the garden was the evanescent kind, the kind that makes even a bird feeder in pieces look like something worth painting. His grandmother came home to a clean-ish kitchen, a plate saved for her, and a grandson narrating the rescue of the lake with his hands. She listened, took a forkful, and said, "You used the good bowl." Lucas waited for the rest of it, but she only looked at his grandfather, who shrugged and went back out to the bird feeder, one screw still loose in his palm.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto of 1848 opens its first section by claiming that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.
story:
The book club met in Sierra's reading nook on Sunday afternoons because her house had the best light and the only copy of Ms. Delgado's annotated Jane Eyre. Four chairs had been dragged in from the kitchen, and the window seat held the kettle, the mugs, and the tin of shortbread that Sierra's mother replenished without comment. Today Alana arrived first, carrying a paperback with a red cover that did not match the stack of novels on the sill.

"Borrowed it from the public library," Alana said. "I got stuck on the assignment, so I went looking for the actual source. It's Marx and Engels, the Communist Manifesto, 1848." She opened it to a page flagged with a receipt. "Listen to this. It opens its first section by claiming that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles."

Elyssa, folding herself into the largest chair with the Brontë in her lap, said, "All of it? Every society ever?"

"That's what it says."

Sierra poured the tea and thought about Mr. Rochester's first entrance, when his horse slips on the ice and he speaks to Jane as though she were a servant, which in that moment she nearly is. She had been trying all week to hold two ideas at once: that the novel was a romance, and that Jane was paid wages, forty pounds a year, to stand in rooms where she would never be invited to sit. The two readings kept sliding apart whenever she tried to write about them.

"Read the beginning again," Sierra said. "The exact words."

Alana read them again, and Sierra copied the sentence onto the inside cover of her notebook, because she did not trust her memory with a claim that large. Then she opened Jane Eyre to the scene where Rochester interrogates Jane about her family, her schooling, her salary, and she read it aloud to the others, stopping where he tells her he pays her thirty pounds and she corrects him to forty.

"That correction," Elyssa said. "She corrects him about her own wage."

"Because the money matters," Sierra said. "The whole book runs on it. Jane is only safe from Mrs. Reed once she has a salary. Her aunt's solvency is failing, and that's part of why Jane gets sent away at all. And when Rochester offers her jewels and dresses before the wedding, she refuses them, because gifts would make her dependent and wages don't." She heard herself speeding up and made herself slow down. "So maybe the line fits. Not that Jane Eyre is about revolution. But every scene in it is somebody with money pressing on somebody without."

Alana frowned at the red paperback. "But it's a love story. The whole point is that she comes back to him."

"She comes back after she's inherited money," Sierra said. "Five thousand pounds, and she splits it with her cousins, and only then, when she doesn't need him, does she go. He's blind and maimed by then, and she has the income. The balance actually tips."

Elyssa looked doubtful in a way that Sierra had learned to trust more than agreement. "So the class reading explains the inheritance," Elyssa said, "but not why she loves him. He's saturnine through half the book, he lies to her, he nearly commits bigamy, and she goes back anyway. Class struggle doesn't cover that."

"No," Sierra said, "it doesn't." She turned her mug a quarter turn on its saucer. That was the part her draft essay had been skating around, the part where the lens lit up certain rooms in the house and left others dark. The wage, the inheritance, the refusal of the dresses, all of it fit. The wanting did not, and the wanting was most of the book.

Ms. Delgado, arriving late with the shortbread her mother had forgotten to buy, was shown the notebook and the red paperback and the two open novels side by side on the window seat. She read Sierra's half-page of notes, the parts underlined twice, and handed it back without correcting anything, which was how she signaled that the thinking was worth continuing. "Your essay doesn't have to pick one," she said, and went to pour her tea.

They finished the chapter they had agreed on, argued about whether the fire in Rochester's bed presaged the events at Thornfield or merely made a good scene, and divided the last of the shortbread. After everyone left, Sierra sat in the nook with both books still open, and wrote at the top of a fresh page: what the wage explains, what it doesn't. Then she underlined it and started on the paragraph about the forty pounds.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Modus ponens is the valid argument form 'if P then Q; P; therefore Q', and it is valid no matter what P and Q stand for.
story:
Avery had claimed the table by the periodicals at four o'clock, before the after-school crowd flooded in, and she spread her debate materials across it like evidence at a trial. The resolution for Saturday was about lowering the voting age to sixteen, and she was arguing the affirmative, which meant she had to prove something she wasn't entirely sure she believed. That was the problem gnawing at her all week: she could feel the truth of it, that sixteen-year-olds pay taxes on their paychecks and drive on the roads and get tried as adults in some courts, yet feeling a truth and building an argument were different crafts altogether.

Brett dropped his backpack on the chair beside her and peeled a clementine without asking how it was going, which was how she knew he could tell it wasn't. Nelly arrived a minute later with two hot chocolates and set one in front of Avery without comment. The three of them had worked this way since freshman year, when Ms. Ferreira had first let them monopolize the corner table on condition they reshelve what they pulled.

"My case is a mess," Avery said. "Every time I write a premise, I hear the other side answering it. If I say sixteen-year-olds are affected by policy, they'll say so are ten-year-olds. If I say we're mature enough, they'll find some study about the prefrontal cortex."

"So make it structural," Brett said, licking juice off his thumb. "Don't argue that we're wise. Argue that taxation without representation is wrong no matter who's taxed. My civics teacher calls that disenfranchisement. You can't disenfranchise a group just because you doubt their judgment, because then you could disenfranchise anyone a majority happens to doubt."

Avery wrote that down, but the pen slowed halfway through. "Except that's exactly what they'll attack. They'll say, fine, if the principle applies to everyone affected by policy, does it apply to felons? To non-citizens? Where does it stop? It's like my logic homework." She dug into her bag and pulled out the worksheet she'd been avoiding, its last problem circled twice in blue ink. "I keep getting these arguments wrong even when I can see they're right, or right when I can see they're wrong, and I can't tell which."

Nelly leaned over and read the problem aloud, half laughing. "If the moose is a librarian, then the trombone is ashamed. The moose is a librarian. Therefore?" She looked up. "This is a joke, right? Someone printed a joke on your homework."

"It's not a joke, that's what's making me insane." Avery stared at the sentences. "If the moose is a librarian, then the trombone is ashamed. Fine. The moose is a librarian. Fine. So the trombone is ashamed. I want to say that's ridiculous, but I can't find where it breaks." She pulled a fresh sheet of paper and, almost to distract herself from the debate, began swapping words. If the radiator is a poet, then the staircase sings opera. The radiator is a poet, therefore the staircase sings opera. She read it aloud, and Brett laughed so loudly that Ms. Ferreira appeared from behind the circulation desk and stood at the end of their table with her cart of returns, saying nothing, merely radiating the patience of someone who had shushed three generations.

"Sorry," Avery said, and then, because Ms. Ferreira had glanced at the worksheet, she slid it toward her. "Is this even a real thing, or did the textbook run out of sentences?"

"It's real," Ms. Ferreira said. "It's called modus ponens." She tapped the shape of it, the if-then, the affirmation, the conclusion, and pushed the sheet back. "You don't have to believe in moose librarians to follow it." Then she rolled her cart on toward biography, having said her piece and no more.

Avery sat very still, because something was assembling itself. "Wait," she said. "Wait. Look at this. It's valid no matter what you put in it. I could put nonsense in the slots all afternoon and it never stops working. The stuff inside can be ridiculous and the argument still holds." She wrote it out again, this time with her own words. If a group is bound by the laws, then it deserves a voice in making them. She stopped, pen hovering. "Except that's where it's different, isn't it. The moose problem is true because of its shape. My premise about laws is only true if you already accept it. The form can be perfect and still carry a premise that half the room rejects."

"So the form is never enough," Nelly said slowly, wrapping both hands around her cup. "But it's also never nothing. It tells you what you still have to defend."

"Which is the premise." Avery drew a box around the if-then line. "So on Saturday I don't spend my time on the conclusion, because that follows. I spend it on the premise, and I concede honestly what I can't prove. I can't prove every affected group should vote. I can't even prove we're ready. But I can show what follows if the principle is granted, and let the judges decide whether to grant it." She heard the shape of her opening statement reforming as she spoke, its old weak claims burning off like fog.

Brett raised his clementine rind in a mock toast. "The trombone is ashamed," he said solemnly, and Nelly snorted into her hot chocolate.

Avery laughed, then bent over the clean page and began writing: If a voice is owed, then sixteen is not too young to hold it. The moose, she thought, would be proud of her. She underlined the premise twice, then stood to reshelve the debate binders, taking the long way past the circulation desk so she could slide the worksheet, the nonsense one with the radiator and the staircase, across the counter to Ms. Ferreira. "For your cart," she said. "Best problem on the sheet."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins; table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius.
story:
The community kitchen on Alder Street opened at four, and by ten past, Rachel had claimed the stove nearest the window because it was the only one whose burner dial she trusted. Her mother was working the late shift at the hospital, her father was two provinces away on a job that kept getting extended, and someone had to make dinner for the family, which tonight meant her and her younger brother. She had planned pork chops, rice, and, because it was his birthday week, a caramel sauce to pour over the vanilla ice cream she had carried home in a bag of frozen peas.

The sauce was the problem. She had made it once before, at home, and pulled it off the heat too early, so it tasted like sweetened water with ambitions. She wanted to get it right this time, which was why she was reading a note on her phone while the sugar sat in the pan, dry and white and stubborn.

The note was from Jaylynn, sent that afternoon from her aunt's place in Belleville.

Hey. My aunt does pastry so I asked her about your sauce thing. She says caramelization is the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins, and table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius. Also she says use a thermometer and stop apologizing to your pans. Good luck. Text me a photo if it works.

Rachel read it twice. She had a thermometer, borrowed from Ms. Sharma, who ran the kitchen on Tuesdays and kept a drawer of equipment that people could sign out like library books. She clipped it to the pan's edge and watched the sugar begin to slump at the edges, turning translucent before it turned anything else.

Lorenzo arrived at half past four with a canvas bag of onions and a plan to make soup, because apparently his family was celebrating something he described only as "a verdict." He set up at the next stove and glanced over at her pan.

"What's the science project?"

"Caramel," Rachel said. "Jaylynn's aunt says the sugar starts to brown at about 170 degrees Celsius, and that it's the sugar on its own, no proteins doing it. So I'm waiting for 170."

"Waiting for a number to happen to your food," Lorenzo said. "That's very patient of you."

The sugar passed 160 and looked like nothing. Then, in the space of what felt like ten seconds but was probably three, it went amber, then copper, and the smell changed from plain sweetness to something darker and almost burnt at the edges. The thermometer read 174. She had wanted to catch it at the first moment of color, and she had missed the first moment; there was no first moment, only a stretch where her attention had lapsed and the pan had gone on without her. She pulled it off the heat, added the cream she had warming in a cup, and the sauce hissed and seized and then, as she stirred, relaxed into something glossy.

Ms. Sharma came by to collect the sign-out sheet and looked into the pan. Rachel expected a correction, some pedagogue's instinct to turn the moment into a lesson, but Ms. Sharma only said, "That's better than most of the ones made in this kitchen," and moved on to argue with Lorenzo about whether his onions needed more time.

Rachel packed the chops and rice and the jar of sauce into her bag, and on the walk home she held the jar up to the streetlights, watching the way it moved, slow and heavy, the color of an old penny. She thought about the number, 170, and how knowing it had not actually saved her; she had still blinked and missed the exact beginning of the change. Knowing a thing and catching a thing were different acts. Maybe next time she would stand with her eyes on the pan and the thermometer as a kind of backup, a second opinion. That felt like a canny arrangement, the instrument and her attention each covering for the other's weakness. Or maybe both were true and neither was enough, and caramel was simply the kind of thing that happened faster than a person could decide about it.

At home her brother was already at the table, and the pork chops went into their own pan with a sound like rain on a tent. When dinner was eaten down to the plates, she scooped the ice cream into bowls and poured the sauce over it, thin at first, then with more nerve.

"It worked," her brother said, mouth full.

Rachel took out her phone and photographed his bowl, then her own, and typed to Jaylynn: It worked. It went from 170 to too dark in about three seconds, so I'm going to watch the pan next time and keep the thermometer anyway. She hit send, and the message sat there with a single checkmark, and her brother held out his bowl for more.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: The Chicago Manual of Style, whose notes-and-bibliography system uses footnotes, was first published by the University of Chicago Press in 1906.
story:
Maelle spread her sources across the corner table of the cafe, four books and a stack of printed articles, and opened her laptop to a document that said, in large gray letters, Argument: The famine was not only a natural disaster. Below that, nothing.

"You've been on that sentence for forty minutes," Javier said. He set down his coffee and pulled out the chair across from her. His own document was eleven pages long, which he mentioned twice.

"I don't know how to argue it. I have quotes that say the blight ruined the crop, and quotes that say the policies ruined the people, and they just sit there next to each other. They don't fight." She turned her laptop so he could see. "Mr. Joseph said a research paper has to take a position, not just report."

Javier leaned in, less to help than to prove he was ahead. "Mine's on the printing press. I found this thing out yesterday. You know footnotes, those little numbers? There's a rulebook for them. The Chicago Manual of Style. It came out in 1906, from the University of Chicago Press. So the rulebook for your footnotes is older than your great-grandparents."

"Nobody's great-grandparents are that old," Maelle said.

"Yours could be. It was 1906. That's a hundred and whatever years before us." He scrolled through his own bibliography with one finger, displaying it. "Anyway, that's why the rules are so weird. They had a whole notes-and-bibliography system back then, all in footnotes, and they never changed it. I'm putting that in my intro. Historicism."

"It's not historicism," Maelle said, but she wrote 1906 on the margin of her notes anyway, because a fact with a date felt more solid than her thesis. Behind the counter, Mr. Joseph, who had lived on their street since before either of them could ride a bike, called out that the wifi password had changed again. Shyanne arrived at the table carrying a smoothie and sat down without asking, which was her habit.

"Tell her," Javier said. "The footnote thing."

"The Chicago Manual of Style, 1906, University of Chicago Press," Shyanne recited. "He's told everyone. He told the cashier." She turned to Maelle. "Why do you look like your dog died?"

"Because I have to prove something and I can't even state it. The books about the biology say one thing, the books about the government say another, and I agree with both, partly, and I think that's not allowed."

Shyanne, who wanted to be a lawyer and treated every table as a place to cross-examine, put down her smoothie. "Which do you agree with more?"

"That's the problem. It depends which chapter. The blight was real, it destroyed the crop, that's just true. But the crop would have been enough for the people if it hadn't been shipped out. So both are true and one of them explains more."

"So say that," Shyanne said.

"Say what, exactly?"

Shyanne waved a hand at her, as if the sentence were on the table and Maelle was refusing to pick it up. Javier tried to cajole her into a shortcut instead: just summarize the two sides, call the question complicated, and take the grade. "Nobody fails a paper for being balanced," he said.

"That's not balanced, that's nothing." Maelle pulled the laptop back and typed while the other two argued about whether lawyers or historians were more annoying. She wrote: The blight caused the crop failure, but the policies caused the famine, because a failed crop only becomes a famine when food leaves the people who grew it. She read it twice. It had a hinge in it, a because, and it could be wrong in public, which made it an argument and not a summary.

"Fine," she said out loud. "Now I need evidence for each half, and the footnote format." She looked at the 1906 scribbled in her margin. "Which, apparently, has rules older than everyone in this building."

Mr. Joseph came over with a cloth to wipe their table, mostly to see what they were working on. "Chicago style," he said, glancing at her screen. "Footnotes at the bottom, bibliography at the end. My professors used to fail you for a misplaced comma." He moved her cup, wiped under it, and stood there a moment.

"Do you know how to do the first one?" Maelle asked. "The note, with the page number?"

He pulled the cloth through his hands. "I might remember," he said. "You buying the next round of coffees?"

Maelle turned the laptop toward him and pulled a second chair around to her side of the table.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The word valedictorian comes from the Latin vale dicere, meaning "to say farewell," which is why the valedictorian gives a farewell speech.
story:
The speech was due at nine the next morning, and Leah had written four words: Hello, graduates, and also. She sat on the hood of her mother's Corolla in the school parking lot, laptop balanced on her knees, watching Sahil and Roland attempt to fit a beach umbrella into the trunk of Roland's hatchback for reasons neither of them had explained.

"You're the valedictorian," Sahil called over, "and you've written 'and also.' That's very judicious of you. One word per week, and you've had, what, five weeks?"

"Six," Leah said. "I'm ahead of schedule."

Roland gave up on the umbrella and let it spring open in the middle of the parking lot, catching a gust and tipping sideways like a drunk flamingo. He wrestled it down while Sahil laughed so hard he had to lean on the Corolla, which rocked Leah and her laptop, and she saved her document out of pure superstition.

"Six words, then," Roland said, collapsing the umbrella with a snap. "You must really not want to graduate."

"That's the problem. I do. That's the whole speech, actually. I have to say goodbye to all of you and I don't know how to do it without sounding like a greeting card that cries."

Mr. Sultani, who taught Latin and had apparently been walking to his car the whole time, paused beside them with his briefcase. He didn't offer advice, which was one of his more endearing habits; he just raised an eyebrow at the umbrella, now lashed to the hatchback's roof with what appeared to be a bathrobe sash.

"Mr. Sultani," Leah said, because an idea had started forming at the edge of her mind, "what does vale dicere mean?"

"To say farewell," he said. He smiled slightly, the way he did when a student asked the exact right question. "It's where valedictorian comes from. The title means the one who says farewell. That's why you give the speech." Then he lifted his briefcase in a small salute and kept walking, leaving Leah to feel that she had either been handed a gift or robbed of a discovery.

She turned back to the laptop. So the entire word, the title she'd worked four years for, the GPA she'd guarded like a dragon guarded gold, was secretly just a job description. She wasn't the smartest person, etymologically speaking. She was the designated goodbye-sayer. The school had essentially hired her to be sad in public.

"Get this," she said, and told Sahil and Roland the whole thing, vale dicere, farewell, the lot. Sahil immediately began composing alternatives: "By your powers combined, I am Captain Farewell." Roland suggested she open with it and let everyone else do the emotional labor.

Leah typed while they argued about whether the umbrella counted as a hat. The two ideas she'd been carrying around all week, the one from her mother, who said a good speech should internalize its message until it stops sounding like a message, and the one from Roland, who said all graduation speeches were just a taxonomy of clichés arranged in a different order, had suddenly stopped competing. They'd lined up behind the Latin. The speech wasn't about being smart. It was about leaving. And a taxonomy of clichés, deployed carefully, was exactly what you used when you meant something too big to say plainly.

She wrote for twenty minutes while the light went orange over the soccer field. When she finished, Sahil read it over her shoulder, which she tolerated because he was her best friend and because the Corolla's hood was not large.

"It's good," he admitted. "It's actually good. You say vale dicere in it and it's not even corny."

"That's because I say it fast," Leah said, "and then I make a joke about how Latin is the only class where I ever got a B."

"That joke is slander," said Roland, who had gotten the B, and who had made her flashcards for the retake anyway.

At nine the next morning, in folding chairs on the football field, Leah stood at the podium with her pages and watched four hundred seniors in identical gowns settle into their seats. She said vale dicere. She said farewell. She made the Latin joke, and Roland laughed loudest, and her mother wiped her eyes before the sad part even started, which was efficient of her.

Afterward, in the parking lot, still in her gown, Leah found Sahil leaning against the Corolla with a wrapped present balanced on the roof. She peeled back the paper. It was a mug that said WORLD'S OKAYEST LATIN STUDENT, and beneath it, in smaller letters, that vale dicere meant to say farewell, so it was engraved with the definition.

"A reference mug," she said. "For the woman who gives references."

"Flip it over," Sahil said.

On the bottom it read, in gold script: But you didn't need that, did you?

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: In countries with low death rates, a total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman is needed to replace the population without migration.
story:
The mist came off the lake in diaphanous curls, thin enough that Oliver could see the far shore through it, and he sat on a stump with his folder of printed population pyramids balanced on his knees, trying to make them give up their secret before the weekend was over. Ms. Harper had assigned the essay before the trip: take a country's pyramid, read its shape, and argue whether that country would need more schools or more nursing homes in thirty years. Oliver had chosen a pyramid with a wide base and steep sides, a young country, and he had written two pages claiming everything was obvious. The problem was the second country, his own, whose pyramid looked like an old beech tree, narrow at the roots, thick in the middle, and his draft kept collapsing whenever he reached the part about the birth rate.

"Come eat," Hubert called from the fire. "Your graphs will still be ugly in ten minutes."

"They're not ugly, they're information." But he closed the folder and went.

The three of them, Oliver, Hubert, and Lyric, had the fire to themselves that evening, since Ms. Harper and the other parent had walked down to the water to check the canoe. Hubert stood up on his log and delivered a mock speech about the superiority of dehydrated stew, all rolling vowels and raised fist, and Oliver laughed even though his oratory was mostly a way of avoiding the dishes. Lyric threw a pinecone at him mid-sentence, which was, Oliver thought, the correct critical response.

Later, when the fire had burned down to coals, Oliver brought the folder back out. "I'm stuck," he said. "Our country's birth rate is falling. Two kids per family. Two parents, two kids. That's steady. That's replacement. So the numbers should hold and we should need the schools. But the pyramid says otherwise, and I can't make the two things agree."

Lyric frowned at the fire. Hubert said, "Two for two sounds even to me," and went to look for more wood, because he was better at fires than at arguments.

Oliver had brought a small stack of loose pages to feed the stove in the morning, drafts and photocopied scraps he had decided were useless. He was sorting them, folding one to wedge under the kettle, when Lyric grabbed his wrist. "Not that one." She flattened it on her knee. It was a page from a textbook, printed off in the library and then buried in his bag and forgotten. She read it aloud, slowly, the way you read something you don't quite believe: "In countries with low death rates, a total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman is needed to replace the population without migration."

The coals popped. Oliver took the page from her and read it again himself, and something rearranged itself behind his eyes. Two was not the number. Two point one was, in places where few people died young, and only if nobody left and nobody arrived. His whole draft had been built on the wrong floor.

"So all those families with exactly two kids," Lyric said, "are still coming up short."

"By a tenth." He stared at the wide base of the young country's pyramid, then at the shrunken base of his own. "Which sounds like nothing. But times everyone." He got out his notebook and crossed out half a page without ceremony.

The twist came at breakfast, when Ms. Harper, going over the route for the hike, mentioned that the valley they were walking through had lost its school ten years ago and kept its care home. "Half the village I grew up in," she said, and pointed up the trail, and left it there. Oliver walked most of the morning slightly behind the others, watching the empty schoolhouse through the trees when they passed it, windows clouded, a rusted bell bracket still on the wall, and the care home beyond it with laundry on the line.

By the lake at noon he sat with his back against a rock and wrote a third draft.
