His first idea had been that the numbers alone decided things, schools or nursing homes, one or the other, like flipping a coin. His second, last night, had been that numbers decided everything and he had simply had the wrong number. Neither was right by itself, he thought, and neither was wrong. The shape of a population told you something real about the future, but the valley had lost its school without any pyramid predicting it, and his own town was putting an addition on its high school while the newspaper ran pieces about the birth rate. Both things were true at once. He wrote his conclusion in the margin where the sun could dry the ink: that a country like his would likely need the nursing homes, and soon, and that what he could not account for was the line in the middle of the copied page, the part about migration, which was not a number at all but a door that people kept walking through in both directions.

He read the last sentence over once, then closed the notebook and skipped a stone flat across the still water, counting the skips until he lost it in the mist.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: Long or repeated exposure to sounds at or above 85 decibels can cause hearing loss, and the damaged hair cells in the human inner ear do not grow back.
story:
Ms. Ivanova had him read his draft aloud at the long table by the library window, and twice she tilted her right ear toward him and said, "Again, please, and slower." Henry had noticed this before, the way she angled her whole body when he spoke, the way she laughed a half beat after everyone else at jokes, as if the laugh were being delivered to her on a delay. She was a retired sound engineer, which was the whole reason the school had paired them; she had mixed live shows for twenty years, and Henry wanted to do the same. He read the paragraph again and watched her cup her hand behind her ear.

"Your essay is turgid in the middle section," she said, tapping the page. "Every sentence carrying two adjectives and a clause it cannot hold. Write like you mix sound. Give the important thing the level it needs and pull everything else down."

He promised he would revise it, and he meant it, but he was barely listening, because his ears were still ringing. It had started Saturday night, at the venue on Carver Street, and it was now Thursday. A thin, steady tone, like a wire somewhere behind his hearing, constant while he ate breakfast and constant while he tried to fall asleep. He had said nothing about it to anyone except Ana, who had been beside him at the barrier in front of the speakers for three hours while Jaxon pressed forward and lost himself entirely, singing with his eyes shut.

After the mentorship meeting he sat on the library steps and texted her. "Still ringing. day 5. should i be worried." He watched the three dots appear and vanish and appear. He thought about asking Ms. Ivanova directly, and then thought about how she turned her ear, and decided he did not want to know what she would say yet.

Her reply came as a long message, the kind she wrote when she'd been reading. "Okay so I looked it up because I was worried too. Long or repeated exposure to sounds at or above 85 decibels can cause hearing loss. And here's the part that got me: the damaged hair cells in the inner ear do not grow back. Ever. Front row at that show was way past 85. I already ordered earplugs, the musician kind that lower everything evenly. Please get some. Consider this me trying to beseech you, because you know you don't listen to me when I just suggest things." He read it twice on the steps, his thumb holding the screen awake, and the wire behind his hearing kept sounding.

He walked to the music store on Halsted that afternoon and paid fourteen dollars for a small plastic case. The cashier, an older man with gray stubble, held them up and said, "Smart. Wish I'd started at your age," and tapped his own ear, where there was a hearing aid the color of his skin that Henry had not noticed until that moment. Henry looked at it for a second longer than politeness allowed, and the man didn't seem to mind.

The next show was two weeks later, the same venue, a different band, and Jaxon saw him screwing the plugs in by the merch table and laughed. "You look like my grandfather at the airport." Jaxon leaned in close, almost beseeching in his mock solemnity, hands spread: "You're eighteen. You can't already be falling apart." Ana appeared at Henry's shoulder and said, "The cells don't grow back," and Jaxon said, "What cells," and she said, "In your ear. Look it up tomorrow," and then the lights went down and there was no more talking.

The strange thing, Henry found, was that the music was better. With the plugs in, he could pick the bass line out of the turgid wall of sound it had been buried in before, could hear the singer land a note he had never once heard live, could feel the kick drum in his chest rather than in his teeth. He stood beside Ana and thought about standing here at forty, at sixty, and about which version of himself he was currently deciding for. That was the thing he hadn't expected: that the plugs were not for tonight at all. Tonight was fine either way. They were for a night twenty years off that he could not picture, some band he hadn't heard yet, some child maybe, saying something across a table, and him tilting his ear, asking for it again and slower.

At their next meeting he told Ms. Ivanova everything, the ringing, the five days, the plugs, and she listened without tilting her head, then took her own hearing aid out and set it on the table between them, a small tan shell, and let him look at it. "You used discernment," she said. "Most people your age think discernment means knowing what's true. It's knowing what matters while there's still time to act on it." He asked her when hers started, and she said, "Gradually. That's the worst part. No single night to point to. You'd have liked a night, something to blame." He said the ringing had finally faded by Sunday, and she nodded and said, "That's how it works. It fades. The damage stays." She slid the aid back in, picked up his revised essay, and said, "Now read it to me again, from the top. Let's hear if you learned to write like you mix."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: The Truman Doctrine, announced in March 1947, pledged US support for countries resisting communist pressure, starting with aid to Greece and Turkey.
story:
Dominic had taped two index cards to his bedroom wall, one above the other, and by Sunday night he had read them so many times they had begun to feel like rivals living in his house. The first was a quotation from a historian named Alperovitz, who ascribed the Cold War chiefly to American economic ambition, arguing that the United States needed open markets and therefore manufactured a Soviet threat. The second, from Gaddis, put the blame on Stalin, an autocrat who answered to no electorate and could pursue whatever course he pleased. Mr. Hoffmann had assigned exactly this question, which explanation the evidence better supported, and had refused to say which one he favored, which Dominic found almost unbearably smug.

The problem was that Dominic had a grandfather instead of an archive. He was driving out Sunday with his mother because she had promised, months ago, that he could look through the boxes of his grandfather's papers, and because his grandfather had actually been alive in 1947, which counted as evidence to Dominic even if it wouldn't to Gaddis.

"You're going to quiz Grandpa on the origins of the Cold War," his mother said from the driver's seat. "He'll tell you it started when the Russians stole his job in 1953."

"He worked in a warehouse. In Ohio."

"I'm just saying he has theories."

His grandfather met them at the door in a cardigan and immediately began building what he called a timeline, pulling a legal pad from a drawer and drawing a long horizontal line with a pencil he sharpened with a knife, which Dominic found both charming and atavistic, like watching someone start a fire without matches. "You want to know when it started," his grandfather said. "Everybody wants a starting date. That's the whole game, isn't it. Where you put the first mark on the line."

Dominic had his phone out, ready to argue. "Some people say it was the Long Telegram," he said. "Kennan sent it in 1946, before anything actually happened. It was just one diplomat saying what he thought the Soviets were like."

"And some people say Truman." His grandfather tapped the empty line. "In March 1947 he stood up in front of Congress and pledged American support for any country resisting communist pressure. They called it the Truman Doctrine. First money went to Greece and Turkey. That's when we stopped pretending we weren't picking a side."

Dominic looked at the pad. "But the speech came after the telegram. If the telegram is the cause, the doctrine is just the effect."

"Or the telegram is the theory and the doctrine is the fact on the ground." His grandfather wrote a small X on the line and then, after a pause, wrote a second X before it, and then a question mark between them, which was either profound or a sign he had lost his place. "A speech with money in it is different from a letter with opinions in it. But don't ask me which one is the start, because I've been arguing that with your grandmother for forty years and she's not here to lose."

Dominic spent the evening in the boxes while his mother and grandfather argued about gutters. He found a newspaper clipping, brittle and brown, about the aid package, and he sat cross-legged on the carpet holding it, thinking that Alperovitz would call the aid a market opening dressed up as rescue, while Gaddis would call it a response to pressure on Greece, and that the clipping itself, with its photographs of ships and senators, was perfectly silent about which was true. Both historians could hold it. That was the thing nobody had warned him about, that evidence didn't always break the tie. He copied the date onto a fresh index card and put it in his pocket.

On Monday he found Amos and Jayde in Mr. Hoffmann's room before the bell, Amos laying out his own timeline on the desk with the Long Telegram printed in enormous font, practically a poster. "Nineteen forty-six," Amos said. "Everything after is just logistics."

"I used to think that," Dominic said, and heard himself sound like his grandfather. "But a telegram is one man's theory. In March 1947 Truman pledged support to countries resisting communist pressure, actual aid to Greece and Turkey. That's a commitment, not an opinion." Jayde pointed out that a commitment had to come from somewhere, and that the somewhere might be exactly what Alperovitz said it was, and for ten minutes the three of them pushed the two marks back and forth along the line the way his grandfather had, with question marks accumulating in between.

Mr. Hoffmann collected their drafts at the end of class, read Dominic's first page standing up, and said, "You've argued that neither explanation is sufficient alone. That's honest. It's also going to be harder to grade." He handed it back with a small X in pencil at the top and, beneath it, a question mark.

"That's it?" Dominic said. "What does the X mean?"

"Ask your grandfather," Mr. Hoffmann said. "He invented it."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In Edgar Allan Poe's 1843 story 'The Tell-Tale Heart', the narrator insists he is not mad while describing how he murdered an old man.
story:
The library smelled of radiator dust and the lemon spray the janitor used on the tables after lunch, and Florence had claimed the corner carrel by the window because it was the only one where nobody could read over her shoulder. In front of her lay the photocopy Ms. Somsak had made of Poe's 1843 story, "The Tell-Tale Heart," its margins already thin with her pencil marks. The assignment was due Thursday. It was Tuesday, and she had nothing but a page of quotations she did not yet understand.

Kiera dropped into the chair across from her without asking, unwrapping a granola bar the way a person unwraps something they intend to share and then doesn't. "You're doing the Poe one too?"

"Everyone's doing the Poe one. There were only eleven copies."

"So what's your argument?" Kiera broke off a piece and ate it herself.

Florence turned the photocopied page toward her. "I keep writing about the murder and then deleting it. The old man dies, fine, that's the plot. But the story is mostly him insisting he isn't mad." She tapped the opening lines. "He says his senses aren't dulled, that his hearing is actually sharpened. He's so busy defending himself." She hesitated, because the thought was still soft at the edges. "It's the protests that make you doubt him. He tells you exactly how he murdered an old man, in detail, in between telling you he's sane, and you stop believing him because of how hard he's trying to be believed."

Kiera chewed for a while. "So the point of view is doing it. If someone else told the story, you'd trust it."

"Maybe. Or maybe not." Florence pulled the page back. "That's what I can't decide."

Ms. Somsak passed their carrel on her way to the returns cart and slowed, the way she did when she was pretending not to eavesdrop. "How's the thesis coming, Florence?"

"Stuck. I have the observation but not the argument."

"Good. Stay stuck a little longer." She moved on toward the cart, and Florence watched her go, remembering the fall, when Ms. Somsak had written on her Jane Eyre essay that Florence's confidence was outrunning her evidence. She had been humiliated then, and grateful later, and she could not decide which of those feelings she was supposed to keep.

Kiera leaned in. "You know what Theresa said? She's writing that the narrator is actually telling the truth, that the heartbeat is real, ghosts and all. Full anachronistic psychological reading, like he's a case study in a modern courtroom."

"That's not the assignment."

"No, but it's fun." Kiera crumpled the wrapper. "The problem with you is you preempt every interesting claim by admitting the counterargument first. You hedge before anyone can argue with you."

Florence opened her mouth to object and found, inconveniently, that she was already composing the concession. She laughed instead, and Kiera laughed, and for a moment the essay receded and they were just two people by a cold window with an afternoon left.

When Kiera left for practice, Florence worked through it alone, writing and crossing out. She tried the position that the narrator's insistence was the mechanism: that Poe had built doubt into the voice itself, so that the reader's mistrust was manufactured by the very sentences asking for trust. Then she tried Theresa's way of reading, holding the ghost heartbeat as real, and found something she hadn't expected: the story got less interesting, because if the narrator was simply accurate, there was nothing to do. The doubt was where the reader lived. She wrote three paragraphs and, for the first time, did not end each one with a sentence taking it all back. She let a claim stand and felt the small vertigo of standing behind it.

She was copying her final quotation when Theresa herself appeared at the carrel, hair damp from the shower, holding her own copy of the story. "Kiera told me you think my reading's a waste of time."

"I didn't say that."

"She said you said it was fun but wrong."

Florence looked down at her page. "I said it made the story less interesting. That's different." She thought of her own essay, of how carefully she had trimmed every assertion to the size of its proof, and she thought of the murderer in the story announcing his sanity. "Actually," she said slowly, "maybe your problem and mine are the same problem. You're deciding he's reliable to have somewhere to stand. I've been refusing to decide so I never have to stand anywhere. He's deciding he's sane so he never has to look at what he did." She heard how it sounded, a neat triangle drawn too fast, and she left it there anyway, undecorated.

Theresa set her copy of the story on the table between them, face down, and Florence noticed for the first time that the pages were annotated in pencil in more than one handwriting, dense and confident, and Theresa's own loose scrawl wandered through the margins like a second, smaller voice.

"Read the inside cover," Theresa said. "Page one, top corner."

Florence turned the photocopy over. There, in fading pencil, in a hand she recognized the way you recognize your own signature on an old permission slip, was her own name from two years ago, when she had read the story alone in this same library and argued, in notes she had entirely forgotten writing, that the narrator was perfectly rational and the old man probably deserved suspicion.

"Theresa, I wrote that?"

"Ms. Somsak keeps all the old annotated copies in the back. She gave me this one and told me to find out who'd written in it." Theresa slid the page toward her. "She said you'd want to see it before you handed anything in."

Florence sat very still, her pencil hovering over three tidy paragraphs she no longer entirely trusted, and outside the window the janitor was unlocking the doors to put the return cart away.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Commencement means "beginning"; the word was used for graduation ceremonies because graduates begin a new status, such as being a bachelor or master.
story:
The party was in Larissa's backyard, where someone had strung lights between the fence and the garage and put a playlist on a speaker balanced in a window. Mackenzie arrived still wearing her gown over her arm, the white fabric folded like a bedsheet, because she hadn't wanted to go home first and see her mother's face doing that proud, weeping thing again. The grass smelled of cut and gasoline. Someone's little brother was running through the sprinkler even though it was almost dark.

"You're late," Larissa said, pressing a red cup into her hand. "Ilyas already gave his toast. It was extremely pithy. Like six words total."

"What were they?"

"'We did it. Now what.'" Larissa shrugged. "Honestly it was better than the valedictorian's." She meant Priya's speech, the one about doors opening, and Mackenzie laughed even though something in her chest had been heavy all afternoon, since the moment the principal said the word and the caps went up.

She found Ilyas sitting on the porch steps with his shoes off, rolling a bottle cap between his fingers. He had been the first person to talk to her in ninth grade, in Ms. Addo's English class, when the teacher made them contextualize a poem by reading the newspaper around it, and he had leaned over and whispered that the poem was about his uncle's street in Karachi better than any article. Four years of sitting together since then, and now he was leaving for Toronto in August and she was staying, and neither of them had said so out loud all night.

"I keep thinking it's over," she said, sitting down beside him. "Like that's the whole thing. Thirteen years and a handshake."

"That's bleak." He flicked the cap into the grass.

"Ms. Addo said something at the rehearsal, though." Mackenzie turned the cup in her hands. "She said don't call it graduation, call it what it actually is. Commencement. I looked it up on my phone during the practice, because I thought she was just being one of those teachers who corrects your vocabulary for sport."

"And?"

"It means beginning. That's all it means." She watched the sprinkler stutter across the lawn, catching the porch light in arcs. "They started using it for these ceremonies because the graduates begin a new status. Like becoming a bachelor, or a master. That's why it's called that. You commence being something else."

Ilyas was quiet for a moment, and she could see him deciding whether to take it seriously. "So the whole ceremony is named after starting over. And you're sitting here mourning it."

"I'm not mourning it," she said, and then heard herself and stopped. "Fine. Maybe I am. It's not the classes I'll miss. It's that this is the last night everybody's in one yard. After tonight everyone scatters and we all become people who used to know each other."

Earlier that week her father had taken her to dinner and talked about the family business, the way he had since she was small, and she had understood for the first time that he wasn't asking her to take it over, he was asking her not to make him feel that his whole working life had been a detour. She had said nothing definite, and he had paid the bill and seemed satisfied, and she had lain awake wondering whether that was kindness or cowardice. Ms. Addo, when Mackenzie had gone back for her calc book on the last day, had said only, "You don't owe anyone an answer you haven't given yourself," and Mackenzie had carried the sentence around since, uncertain whether it was permission or evasion.

"Here's what I don't get," Ilyas said. "You're sad it's ending, and you're staying here, so technically nothing's ending for you. Same town, same people."

"It ends anyway. I'll be at community college and everyone will be at universities and by December nobody will text back. That's how it works. My sister's friends all dissolved like that." She remembered her sister's graduation party in this same kind of yard, how certain those girls had looked, and how one of them now sold insurance in a strip mall. Mackenzie had always thought of that as a sad ending, and now, hearing the word commencement turning over in her head, she wondered whether it had just been a beginning nobody had bothered to name.

"Or," Ilyas said, "you could be wrong about that. You're wrong about things occasionally."

"Name one."

"The junior year history essay. You argued America was becoming a plutocracy and I said it was more complicated than rich people running everything, and Ms. Addo gave me the higher mark."

"That's one thing," she said, but she was smiling, and the heaviness in her chest had shifted, not lifted exactly, but redistributed, the way weight moves when you turn a coin over. Maybe both things were true at once, that it was an ending and a beginning, and neither one cancelled the other out. She didn't know yet whether she would take over the shop, or whether she would transfer to a university in two years, or whether the friends would dissolve, and she was surprised to find she could hold all that not-knowing in her hands without dropping the cup.

Larissa came out onto the porch with a plate of cake. "You two are doing that thing where you sit in the dark solving the world. Come dance, the sprinkler's off, the lawn's wet, it's perfect."

Mackenzie stood, brushed the grass from the back of her dress, and left her gown folded on the steps, a white square in the dark. Then she followed Larissa barefoot onto the wet lawn, where Ilyas was already standing with his arms up, waiting for the next song to start.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: Andrew Wakefield's 1998 paper in The Lancet claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism was based on only twelve children.
story:
The library smelled of carpet cleaner and old glue, that particular odour that clung to the backs of Maelle's hands by the end of a long afternoon. She had claimed the corner table by the window, the one with a wobbly leg she steadied with a folded napkin, and spread out her materials like a surgeon: two photocopied articles, a highlighter gone soft at the tip, a notebook open to a page headed only with a question mark. Mr. Charles, the librarian with the jaundiced cast to his reading glasses, had pulled the second article from the bound periodicals that morning and slid it across the desk without comment, though he had paused over her first choice with one eyebrow raised.

The first article had been easy to find. It came up everywhere when she searched, cited and re-cited, the study that had launched a decade of fear. The second one, a population study that had followed hundreds of thousands of children, had taken her two days and one embarrassing email to her old biology teacher to track down. Both addressed the same question, her assignment sheet said: whether the MMR vaccine and autism were linked. Her task was to weigh them against each other, and she had assumed the weighing would be the hard part.

Donovan dropped into the chair across from her without asking, peeling the foil off a muffin he had smuggled past the front desk. "You've been here since lunch," he said. "Your table looks like a crime scene."

"It kind of is one." She turned the first article toward him and tapped the methods section, where she had highlighted the same phrase three times without quite believing it. "Look at this. Look at what it's built on."

He leaned in, chewing. "Twelve kids?"

"Twelve." She said the number out loud again, testing it. "That's it. That's the whole foundation." She slid the second article beside it, its density of tables and follow-up figures fanning across the table like a dropped hand of cards. "And then there's this one. Same question, completely different scale." She sat back. "How did anyone read the first one and not ask immediately how small it was? Twelve. My grade nine class had thirty-one people in it."

Donovan shrugged and broke off a piece of muffin. "Maybe they did ask. Maybe asking didn't matter once the story got loose." He said it lightly, but Maelle wrote it down anyway, because it was the first thing all day that had felt like a hinge. She had spent the morning trying to decide which article was right, as if the assignment were a verdict, and only now noticed that the more interesting sentence was a different one: not which one is true, but why did the smaller one travel so much farther?

Alexanne arrived at four, hair damp from the pool, and read over Maelle's shoulder while eating a bag of rice crackers with unnecessary volume. "Your draft says the second study is more reliable," she said.

"Does it?" Maelle read her own paragraph and frowned at it. The word reliable sat there looking simpler than it should. "I wrote that this morning. I'm not sure it's the whole thought anymore." She pulled the notebook toward her and started a fresh page. "It's more reliable, yes. But that's almost the boring part. The part I keep snagging on is how they even belong in the same sentence. One of them asks a question of twelve children. The other asks it of a whole country. And they both got printed, both got called evidence, both got read by the same people."

"So say that," Alexanne said, crumbs on her sleeve.

"It's not a verdict, though. My teacher wants a position."

"Then take one and admit the cracks." Alexanne tapped the page. "You're allowed to hold a position and still wonder about something. Nobody executes you for a wondering paragraph."

Maelle laughed, and Mr. Charles glanced over from the circulation desk with a look that suggested execution remained an option for noise violations. She lowered her voice and bent over the page. She wrote fast, in her own vernacular first, the version with too many commas and the phrase so basically at the start of every second sentence, because that draft was for her and the clean one could come later. The position took shape as she wrote it: the larger study deserved the weight of the conclusion, and the smaller one, for all its fame, had been asked to carry more than twelve children could bear. And then, at the bottom, the wondering: what makes a claim travel, and whether size of evidence is even the thing we should be measuring, or whether she was only dazzled by big numbers the way other people were dazzled by scary ones. She underlined the question twice.

She looked up. The window had gone amber, the parking lot below filling with headlights, and Donovan was stacking her articles into a neat pile she would have to unstack.

"Take the twelve with you," Alexanne said, zipping her bag. "It fits in your pocket, kind of. That's probably the problem."

Maelle slipped the first article into her backpack, folded once, and pressed the zipper shut.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: MLA style cites sources in the text with the author's name and page number in parentheses, and lists the full sources at the end under the heading 'Works Cited'.
story:
The cafe had one outlet that worked, and Mallory had claimed it for her laptop before Ryan had even taken off his jacket. Christophe was already at the corner table with a stack of printed pages arranged in a grid, which was his way of pretending he had a system. Ryan set down his coffee and unfolded the essay across the remaining space: eight pages on the Haymarket affair, footnoted, with a page at the end headed "Works Cited."

"Let me guess," Mallory said, not looking up. "History paper."

"Two guesses." He slid it toward Christophe. "Ms. Hernández handed it back with one comment. One."

Christophe held the last page at arm's length, the way a jeweler examines a stone. "She wrote 'bibliography?' with a question mark. Very economical."

"She circled the heading twice." Ryan turned his cup in its ring of condensation. "It's the third draft. The argument's fine, she says. The argument is fine and the heading is wrong, and I don't understand what the difference is."

Mallory spun her laptop around, because she could never resist an audience. "This is an English paper," she said. "We're doing in-text citations, which in MLA means the author's name and page number in parentheses, like (Ellis 44), right in your sentence. Then the full sources all go at the end under the heading 'Works Cited.' That exact phrase. Ms. Hernández wants a heading for a whole list of sources."

"Ryan's problem," Christophe said, "is that he's still writing like it's English class. Footnotes at the bottom of the page, everything numbered."

"So history wants a bibliography at the end, numbered notes, and English wants the name and page in parentheses and a page called 'Works Cited,'" Ryan said. He wrote this on a napkin, then looked at it as though it had betrayed him personally. "They're citing the same sources. Haymarket doesn't change depending on the classroom."

"That," said Mallory, "is the most doctrinaire thing you've ever said, and you once argued for twenty minutes about the correct way to load a dishwasher."

"It's not doctrinaire to want one way of doing a thing."

"It's the definition of it," Christophe said, and pulled the draft toward himself with the pencil he kept behind his ear for ceremonial purposes. "Look. Your second paragraph. You quote the prosecutor saying the anarchists 'selected murder as their means.' Where'd you get it?"

"Foner. Page 212." Ryan found it in his stack of photocopies, which were in no order at all, and which he had been telling himself for two weeks he would organize.

"Fine. So under the other system you just write it out: Foner, in parentheses, 212. Right there. The reader's eye never leaves the sentence." Christophe demonstrated on the margin, his handwriting small and ruthless. "And the footnotes move down to the end, all together, before the bibliography."

Ryan looked at the penciled sentence, then at his own version, where the quotation floated above a little numbered flag. "It does read faster," he admitted. "But the footnote tells you more. My note has the full citation and a comment about the trial record being disputed."

"Then keep the comment. You can put extra material in a note, you just can't call the final page 'Works Cited.'" Christophe said it with the flat authority of someone who had lost a full grade point to this exact distinction in September. "I prognosticate you will fight this until midnight and then do it in one hour, because that is what you did with the outline, and the thesis, and the dishwasher."

Mallory, meanwhile, had gone quiet over her own screen, which for Mallory meant an emergency. "Can I ask something that isn't about Haymarket?" she said. "My English teacher wants us to interview someone about our topic. Oral history. Anyone with actual knowledge." She paused in a way she clearly considered casual. "Ms. Hernández knows about labor history, doesn't she?"

"You want me to introduce you to my history teacher so you can interview her for another class," Ryan said.

"I want to interview a person with knowledge, and that person is two doors from your locker."

"She's going to see through that in about a second."

"She'll see through it," Mallory agreed, already drafting the email, "and she'll say yes anyway, because she likes being asked." She typed a sentence, deleted it, retyped it identically, and seemed satisfied. Her want was simple and unembarrassed, which was more than Ryan could say for his own, lately.

He spent the next hour converting citations on the cafe's unreliable wifi, reading each quotation aloud to himself under his breath. Around the tenth one, he stopped arguing. The parentheses were quicker to read; the notes were better for the two places where the sources genuinely disagreed about what had been said at the rally. He kept those notes long, with his own reasoning folded in, and stripped the rest down to bare references. It wasn't one way or the other. It was the argument in the sentences and the disputes in the back, each in the place where it did its work.

At the end he retyped the final page, single-spaced, alphabetical, and left the old heading in place for a moment before deleting it, letter by letter, the way you tear off a bandage slowly for no reason. When he printed it at the counter, the cashier asked if he wanted the good paper and he said no, this one was doomed either way.

Ms. Hernández returned it Thursday with a checkmark beside the bibliography and, in the margin of page six, one further comment: "The note on the disputed trial record. Good. Expand this." She had underlined "expand" twice.

He showed it to Mallory at the cafe, and she leaned over his shoulder, still radiant from her interview, which had run forty minutes over and produced, by her account, a monologue about newspaper bias that she intended to quote in full. "So you fixed one thing," she said, "and now she wants the part you almost cut."

Ryan folded the draft along its crease and set it under his coffee, 212 already penciled beside the prosecutor's words. "I'll expand the note," he said. "That part, I'm keeping in the back."

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: In The Old Regime and the Revolution, published in 1856, Alexis de Tocqueville argued the Revolution continued the centralization of power already begun under the French monarchy.
story:
The library closed at nine, and Mackenzie had until then, and only until then, because the essay was due at eight the next morning and her printer at home had been moribund for weeks, coughing out half-legible pages before giving up entirely. She spread her sources across the long table by the periodicals: three books on the French Revolution, a folder of photocopies, a laptop with a document titled only "draft" that contained two paragraphs she had written on Sunday and hated by Wednesday.

The assignment was the problem. Mr. Sinclair had not asked what caused the Revolution or whether it was justified; he had asked how views of it had changed since 1800, which meant she could not simply tell the story. She had to tell the story of the storytelling, and every time she tried to introspect her way toward a thesis, she found herself just describing events again, the storming of the Bastille, the Terror, Napoleon, as if narrating hard enough would count as analysis.

Anas dropped into the chair across from her with a stack of his own books and a granola bar he split in half without asking. "Still on the historians thing?"

"Still on the historians thing." She turned her laptop so he could see the paltry document. "I've got this one guy, from like 1856, saying the Revolution wasn't really a break at all. Tocqueville. In The Old Regime and the Revolution, he argued the Revolution just continued the centralization of power the French monarchy had already started. Same machinery, new owners, basically."

"Wait, that's it," Anas said, mouth half full. "That's your paper. You've got the old view, the Revolution as this huge rupture, birth of modern liberty, all that, and then this guy comes along sixty years later and says nothing fundamental changed. That's a change in views right there. You just put them next to each other."

"Mr. Sinclair says putting things next to each other isn't the same as having a position."

"Then have a position."

"About which?" She kept her voice low, because the reference librarian had already glared at them once. "Whether he was right, or whether the earlier view was right, or whether either of them could see straight from where they stood? I don't know enough to know that."

She did know one thing, though, and it had been bothering her since the spring. Flashback: the class trip in April to the provincial archives house, a building that had been an intendancy under the old monarchy, where royal officials had once collected taxes and filed reports on their neighbors. The guide had mentioned, almost in passing, that after 1789 the revolutionary committees had moved into the same offices, kept the same files, sent the same kinds of reports to Paris. Mackenzie had stood in the hallway with its worn stone floor and thought, not in words yet, that the room had simply changed hands. She hadn't known Tocqueville's name then. Now the two things clicked together in her head, the argument on the page and the hallway she had actually walked through, and she pulled the laptop back and started typing faster than she had all week.

Maddox arrived at seven-thirty with a milkshake and no books, because Maddox had finished his essay on Monday and considered this a personality trait. "You're still here? You're going to be one of those people who lives in the library. A hedonist of the index card."

"That's not what hedonist means," Anas said.

"It means someone who loves pleasure. Books are his pleasure. Keep up."

"I'm at six hundred words," Mackenzie said, not looking up. She was writing the paragraph where she admitted the limit of her own argument: that a reused building proved continuity of administration, but said nothing about what people believed, and belief was where the older historians had located the rupture, in the sudden conviction that sovereignty belonged to the nation. She had tried to bring the two perspectives together, Tocqueville's continuity and the rupture school's ideology, into one considered position, and the honest version of that position had a hole in it, and she had decided, on Anas's advice, to write the hole into the paper rather than around it.

At ten to nine the lights flicked once, the librarian's signal. Maddox gathered her books while she saved the file twice and emailed it to herself, and Anas held the door. Outside, the November air bit at their ears, and Maddox asked whether she'd actually finished.

"I finished something," she said. "Whether it's the right thing, I'll find out at eight a.m." She zipped her bag, and the three of them walked toward the bus stop, their breath making small clouds under the streetlight.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guideline, normal adult blood pressure is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic.
story:
The cuff hissed, the needle fell, and Olivier read the screen again as though it might apologize. His father had left the monitor on the bathroom shelf that morning, next to the shaving cream, with a sticky note in his blunt handwriting: Thursday, before coffee. The number on the screen was 118 over 76, and Olivier had no idea whether to be relieved.

He had offered to help with the monitoring the way you offer to carry groceries, casually, but the offer had catalyzed something in the household. His father, who had laughed off the clinic appointment for weeks, now took readings like a man taking temperatures of a feverish child. His mother had stopped putting the salt cellar on the table without saying anything about it. Nobody had explained anything to Olivier, which was, he suspected, why he was standing barefoot on the cold tiles at seven in the morning with a textbook open on the closed toilet lid.

The chapter in the book was more direct than his family. Under the 2017 American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guideline, it said, normal adult blood pressure was below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic. He copied the numbers onto the back of his hand, then, feeling eleven years old, onto a fresh sticky note of his own.

He also had to present this in Mr. Mensah's class on Friday, which was the part that kept him awake. The assignment said interpret a reading and explain how diet and exercise change it, and Mr. Mensah had been blunt about what he wanted: not a recitation but an interpretation, a boy standing in front of his classmates saying what a number meant and what could move it.

At school, Olivier claimed the third-floor bathroom before lunch because it was quiet and because the mirror gave him someone to fail in front of. He set the note on the edge of the sink, ran the tap to cover the sound of his own voice, and started.

"Under the 2017 guideline," he told his reflection, "normal is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic. Which means, if you're looking at 118 over 76," and here he faltered, because the sentence wanted to end in something certain and he did not feel certain.

The door opened. Rayhan came in with Dina behind him, both of them mid-argument about the seating plan for the diploma ceremony, and both of them stopped when they registered Olivier addressing the mirror.

"We're not interrupting something private," Dina said. "We're interrupting something public and embarrassing."

"118 over 76," Olivier said. "That's the reading from this morning. My dad's. Is that good?"

"Systolic, diastolic," Rayhan said, pointing at the two numbers, helpfully, before losing his nerve. "That's which is which."

"First one's the systolic," Olivier said. "Under the guideline it has to be below 120, and the second one below 80, for normal. So 118 over 76 is inside it. Barely, on the top number, but inside."

Dina leaned against the partition and studied him. "You don't sound happy about that."

"It's one reading. Tuesday it was 124. Monday my mom rearranged the kitchen and he ate something with no taste and it was 122. I don't know if it's the food or the walking or just the machine." He turned the tap off. "Mr. Mensah wants me to say diet and exercise change the numbers, and I believe that, I do, but I can't tell my dad which thing did what. I can only say the reading moves when the life moves."

"So say that," Rayhan said. "Say the reading follows the living."

Dina had gone quiet in the way she did when she was taking somebody's inventory. She slid off the partition, cupped water in both hands, and drank, which was her way of buying time. "My grandmother had this," she said finally. "The whole family turned into cardiologists for a year and then nobody talked about it again. What helped her wasn't the numbers. It was that my uncle learned them and then sat with her while she measured. You're doing that part already."

Olivier looked at the sticky note, curling slightly in the steam from the tap. The detente in his house, the unspoken truce between the salt cellar and the walking shoes, might not be a solution so much as a way of living while one assembled itself. He could stand in front of the class and say the threshold, say that 118 over 76 sat inside it by two points, and say honestly that what moved the number next month he could not promise, only that it answered to how his father lived, in ways he would keep watching for.

"Friday," he said to Dina and Rayhan, folding the note into his pocket. "You're both sitting in the front row so I have somewhere to look."

Rayhan clapped him once on the shoulder, and Dina said, "Front row, and if you freeze, I'll mouth the words 'below 120' at you like a coach." She pulled the door open, and the hallway noise rushed in around them.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The antiderivative of 1 over x is the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x, which fills the one gap the power rule leaves.
story:
Mya sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with the textbook open to a page of curves, her grandmother's coffee going cold beside her elbow. The house smelled of lavender and old paper, and through the window the garden had gone sullen in the November rain, the roses bowed over like students caught cheating. She had been sent here for the week because her mother said she needed quiet before the exam, though really her mother needed the apartment to herself and the new baby, and Mya had agreed too quickly to pretend it was about calculus.

The problem had followed her anyway. She wrote it at the top of the page: the integral of one over x, dx. Around it she had drawn arrows, abandoned half-steps, a power rule attempt scratched out so hard the paper had torn. The power rule worked for everything, she had believed. Add one to the exponent, divide by the new exponent. She tried it once more in the margin, knowing it would fail, and it failed in the same strange way it had failed in class: the exponent went to zero, and there was nothing left to divide by.

Finnegan had told her, on the bus in September, that calculus was a language for liars. "You can make anything sound true if you wave an integral at it," he'd said, and she had laughed, but she thought about it now while the rain ticked against the glass. Ms. Popal, her teacher, was of the opposite persuasion. On the first day she had said that the subject had probity, that it was one of the few places where a claim had to show its work or be thrown out, and Mya had written the word in her notebook because she liked the sound of it and did not know it yet. Both of them were right, she suspected, and she could not see how.

She texted Stacey, who was also at a relative's house for the holiday, and Stacey sent back a photograph of her own page, which was blank except for the problem copied out neatly, like a confession with no crime attached. "I keep getting zero or infinity," Stacey wrote. "There has to be something else." Mya set the phone face down and pulled the textbook toward her again, because she wanted to be the one who found it, and that want was embarrassing and true.

In the back of the book, in a section they had not been assigned, she found the answer printed like a small verdict. The antiderivative of one over x is the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x. She read the line four times. She had been applying the power rule to every function shaped like one over a power, and this one was the hole in that method, the single case it could not touch. The logarithm stepped into the gap like a substitute player who had been waiting at the side of the pitch the whole game. She checked the claim against nothing, because there was nothing in the book but the claim itself, and she understood suddenly that accepting it was a kind of trust, which was the part Ms. Popal never mentioned and Finnegan was probably right about.

She thought of her grandfather, before he died, sequestering himself in this same kitchen with his stamp collection, sorting the world's small rectangles into albums by country and decade. He had shown her once how a single stamp could belong in two places, and how he chose one, and how the choosing was the whole hobby. She had been nine and had thought it was boring. Now she sat where he had sat, and the choice between trusting the printed rule and distrusting it felt strangely like that, like something you did with your hands even though it was really about what you believed.

"Supper," her grandmother called from the hallway, and Mya went and ate stewed chicken and rice and let the conversation drift over her, answering when asked about the baby, about school, about whether the room was warm enough. Afterward she dried the dishes while her grandmother washed, and the window over the sink held her reflection and the dark garden behind it.

Back at the table, she started the problem again from nothing. She wrote the integral, then the answer, then, underneath, in her own handwriting: "The antiderivative of one over x is the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x, which fills the one gap the power rule leaves." Saying it that way made it hers, or made her responsible for it, and she could not tell the difference. She tested it on an area under a curve from one to four, drew the trapezoid she could have approximated by hand, and watched the logarithm's number land inside the range she had guessed. That was not proof. She knew it was not proof. It was a witness agreeing with a witness.

She messaged Stacey the line, and Stacey replied with three exclamation marks and then, a minute later, "wait why," and Mya typed "power rule breaks there" and deleted it and typed "just doesn't work for that one" and deleted that too. Finally she wrote, "I don't fully know yet. I know that it's true." She read the sentence before sending it, and it seemed to hold both positions at once, the way her grandfather held two albums open on his knees, and she sent it.

Her grandmother passed through on her way to bed and paused at the table, squinting at the curves. "That looks like the side of a hill," she said, tapping the page. Mya looked where the finger pointed. "That's sort of what it is," she said. "I'm finding the area under it." Her grandmother nodded slowly, then turned off the kitchen light, leaving only the small lamp over the stove, and Mya bent back over the page in the amber glow, pencil moving through the next problem.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: In Judaism, a day begins at sundown, so a Seder or a Sabbath dinner is held on the evening that starts the holiday, not the evening that ends it.
story:
Luca had told everyone, twice, that he had learned the whole order by heart, and for most of the afternoon he half believed it himself. He stood in his aunt's kitchen with the Haggadah open on the counter, the one his grandfather had used for forty years, its spine cracked and its margins full of handwriting he could barely decipher. Cousins crowded the hallway. His mother was being a sycophant about his parsley chopping, calling it restaurant quality, which it was not, and the smell of the brisket filled the whole apartment the way it had filled his grandfather's house before the man shrank into a chair and stopped leading anything.

The trouble had started on Tuesday, when Luca went to the community centre and booked the small hall downstairs for the family. He had been proud of himself for that. He'd booked it for Friday evening, because in his mind the holiday was Friday and the dinner belonged at the end of it, the way a birthday ends with cake. It was only when Elina, who sat beside him in world history, glanced at his planner and frowned that anything shifted. "Friday night," she said, and then, quieter, "you know a Jewish day starts at sundown, right? The Seder is the evening that begins the holiday, not the one that ends it." Luca had laughed, a short strange sound, and then had not laughed, because the paper in his hand said Friday and the paper said 6 p.m. and he was suddenly cold in a warm classroom.

He had wanted to argue with her. Some part of him, the part that had been rehearsing the Four Questions into his phone's voice memos, wanted to insist that he of all people knew when his own family's holiday began. But the truth, which he turned over all the way home on the bus, was that he had never had to know. His grandfather had simply appeared at the right hour, holding the right cup, and the evening assembled itself around him like iron filings around a magnet. Luca had assumed that leading meant speaking, and now he understood that most of it had been invisible.

The hall was the concrete problem. He had called the centre Wednesday morning and the woman at the desk had said, not unkindly, that Thursday evening was taken but that he could have the room Thursday afternoon until six, or Friday in the morning. Neither worked. So he had gone to his aunt, the one with the small apartment and the large opinions, and had asked, in a voice he tried to make casual, whether the family could come a day early, to her place, and had watched her face do something complicated before she said of course, of course, her mother's tablecloth still fit if you folded it right. He never told her why. He let her believe it was about his grandfather's knees and the stairs at the hall.

Now, at the table, with eighteen people seated and the candles lit, Luca discovered a second problem, which was that he did not actually know the whole order by heart. He knew pieces. He knew the words to the questions because he had drilled them, but the handwashing, the breaking of the middle matzah, the point where you lean, all of it had been scenery to him before, and scenery does not teach you cues. His uncle, three seats down, kept starting to help and then stopping himself, hands hovering, and Luca understood that the whole table was doing that, holding itself back the way you do around a child carrying something full.

There was a moment, during the story of the four children, when Luca's voice caught on the word destitute. "Our ancestors were destitute," he read, because the newer translation at the bottom of the page said that, and he had never noticed that word there before, had never connected the paper-thin crackers and the salt water to people with nothing, and he had to pause because the word was suddenly very heavy in his mouth. His grandfather, who had arrived late with a blanket over his shoulders, was watching him from the far end. Luca could not read the look. He had told his grandfather on the phone that everything was under control, that he had arranged the room himself, and in a technical sense he had, though arranged was perhaps a generous verb for a mistake repaired by an aunt's folding table.

Elina had asked, on Thursday, whether he wanted her to come and stand near him in case he got stuck, and Luca had said no thank you with a firmness that surprised them both. He thought about that firmness now. It had felt like dignity at the time, but turning it over during the blessing over the wine, he could see it might have been pride, the same pride that had booked the wrong evening without asking anyone, the pride of a boy who wanted to be seen leading more than he wanted to lead well. Or perhaps it had simply been the necessary stubbornness of someone doing a hard thing. He held both possibilities and did not resolve them, because the cup was lifting and the room was lifting with it.

What he did know, with a certainty that steadied his hands, was why the meal was tonight and not tomorrow. Sitting between his little cousins, who had asked him why they were doing this on Thursday when school hadn't even let out yet, he had said, "The day starts at sundown, so tonight is when the holiday begins." His youngest cousin had chewed on that, literally, a corner of matzah going soft in her mouth, and then announced it to the table as her own discovery, and no one corrected her, and Luca let her have it.

After the meal, when the tables were being cleared and his aunt was wrapping leftovers in foil with the efficiency of a woman who had fed armies, his grandfather came around the corner of the kitchen holding the old Haggadah. He set it in Luca's hands and closed Luca's fingers over it with both of his own. "Next year," his grandfather said, and then he stopped, the way he had stopped all evening, halfway into sentences, and he looked at Luca over their joined hands, waiting, as if the rest of the sentence belonged to Luca now.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
story:
Eli slid the tray of chicken breasts out of the oven and set it on the potting bench his father had dragged beside the grill, because the kitchen was being repainted and the whole meal had been exiled to the backyard. He had offered to cook dinner two weeks ago, on the evening his mother came home late from the hospital again, and the offer had hardened into a standing arrangement, Thursdays were his. He was not sure yet whether he had offered for altruistic reasons or because he liked standing at the windowless end of the house where nobody asked him about college deposits.

"Are you going to stab it or are you going to cook it?" Matteo called from the fence, where he sat with a can of soda and his sneakers hooked on the middle rail. He had come over ostensibly to help but had so far contributed commentary only.

"I'm checking it," Eli said. He cut into the thickest breast with the tip of a paring knife and peered at the interior, which looked done, more or less, the pink gone to white, the juices running clearish. His father, who was sweeping paint flecks off the porch steps, set the broom against the railing and came down into the grass.

"Don't go by the color," his father said. "Hand me the thermometer." He fished the probe out of the drawer of the potting bench, the one that also held twine and dead pens, and held it out, handle first, the way he had once held out a car key.

Eli took it. "What am I looking for?"

"One sixty-five," his father said. "That's what the food safety agencies say, chicken is safely cooked when the internal temperature reaches a hundred and sixty-five degrees Fahrenheit, about seventy-four Celsius, measured with a thermometer like that." He nudged the tray closer with one knuckle. "Stick it in the thickest part, not touching the bone."

Eeli did as he was told, sliding the probe into the center of the breast he had already cut. The numbers climbed and settled, and he watched them settle, and they stopped at 158. He stood there with the reading in front of him, thinking about how confident he had been thirty seconds earlier, how the color had argued a whole case to him and he had believed it without cross-examination. "It's not there yet," he said.

"That's why you don't stab it first, either," his father said, taking the broom back up. "Now it'll dry out. Put them back in for a bit."

Matteo raised his soda in a small toast from the fence. "Congratulations, you've been cooking by vibes."

Eli returned the tray to the oven, which sat on the extension cord, humming in the dusk, and crouched beside it with the thermometer in his hand. He was thinking of Ms. Koné, his chemistry teacher, who had once told the class that measurement was a form of humility, that instruments existed because human senses were confident charlatans, flattering themselves in every reading. He had liked the sentence without fully agreeing with it. The cut breast had looked done. His eyes had delivered testimony. But the testimony was wrong by seven degrees, and the thermometer had no opinion at all, only a number, and the number was the one thing in the yard that evening that was not trying to extenuate anything.

He remembered, too, an argument from the winter, the one he and his father had never finished, about whether he should take the loan and go to the far school or stay close and commute. His father had said staying was practical, and Eli had heard, underneath, something about the hospital and the late shifts, though his father had not said it and Eli had not asked. He had gone by the surface then, the way he had gone by the color of the chicken, certain of what he was seeing. He crouched in the grass and admitted to himself that he did not know whether the two situations were alike at all, or whether he was dressing up one hesitation in the borrowed clothes of another.

"Timer," Matteo said, pointing. "Or the birds come back out overcooked."

Eli pulled the tray out again after a few minutes, set it on the bench, and pushed the probe into the thickest part of an uncut breast, careful to keep it away from the bone. The display ran upward and stopped, and this time it read 167, past the mark, safely past it, and he said the number out loud partly for his father on the steps and partly for himself. He laid the probe down and started spooning rice onto the paper plates his mother had set out before she left for her shift, and he was still deciding, as he folded the foil over the two plates he would leave warming for her, whether he would text Matteo tonight or make the deposit tomorrow or do neither, when his father said, "Plates, then, before it goes cold," and Eli carried them across the darkening grass.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: On the practical driving test in Great Britain, parallel parking at the side of the road is one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner may ask a candidate to do.
story:
Kate had practised nothing but bay parking for three months, reversing neatly between the painted lines of the leisure centre car park until the manoeuvre felt less like driving than like folding laundry. It was her father who had taught her that way, on the reasonable grounds that she would spend her life in car parks, and she had accepted it the way she accepted most of his reasonable grounds, without checking whether they covered the whole map. The map, she discovered on a wet Tuesday evening in the garage, wiping her hands on an old towel while the kettle ticked behind her, did include the road.

She had gone into the garage to find the torch, and instead she had found the printed booklet from the test centre, left on the shelf beside the WD-40. On the practical driving test in Great Britain, she read, parallel parking at the side of the road was one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner may ask a candidate to do. She read it twice, then a third time, and something in her chest tilted like a shelf coming loose from its bracket.

"You look like you've seen a ghost," said Mr. Mensah, who had come through the connecting door to borrow the step ladder and was now leaning against the freezer with his arms folded. He was the sort of neighbour who treated the garage as shared territory and had once spent forty minutes explaining to her the differences between various engine oils, which he called the hedonism of machines, a phrase she had never fully unpacked.

"I've been practising the wrong thing," Kate said. "Bay parking only. The whole time."

"And the test can ask for a parallel park instead?"

"At the side of the road. It's one of the reversing manoeuvres they can ask for." She said it flatly, testing it, and the words sat in the cold air between them like a verdict.

That night she texted Meghan, because Meghan had passed her test in March and had since developed the lugubrious authority of a war veteran. You did bay parks only, Kate typed, do they definitely ask parallel sometimes? Meghan's reply arrived in three instalments: first a single crying-laughing face, then "my examiner made me parallel park behind a hearse," then "a HEARSE Kate. I nearly joined the deceased." Kate laughed out loud alone in the kitchen, then screenshotted it, then set it as her motivation, the way other people used pictures of mountains.

The next evening she moved the bins out to the kerb as markers and backed the family car between them, over and over, while Sydney stood on the pavement scoring each attempt with a number card she had made from a cereal box. Sydney held up a 3. "You're not turning late enough," she said. "Also you just incapacitated the recycling." Kate got out, righted the bin, and tried again, and the sixth time the card said 6, and the ninth time Sydney forgot to hold it up at all because she was watching, actually watching, and that was how Kate knew.

Her father came out on the fourth evening and stood where Mr. Mensah had stood, arms folded, saying nothing, which from him was a kind of applause. Later, in the garage, he watched her top up the washer fluid and said, "I taught you what I use." She nodded. It wasn't an apology and she didn't need one; it was a man admitting his map had edges. She was honest enough with herself to know she might still fail, that the examiner might ask for something she hadn't drilled, that three evenings of kerb work were not three months of anything. But she also knew something she hadn't known on the wet Tuesday: that a person could read the actual requirements, find the gap in her own preparation, and close it herself, without waiting to be taught the right thing by someone who had happened to think of it.

On the morning of the test she parallel parked behind a white van on a quiet street, smooth and slow, tyres nowhere near the kerb, and when the examiner said, "That's fine, move off when you're ready," she checked her mirror, signalled, and pulled out.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Under joint and several liability, each of several people who share an obligation can be held responsible for the entire amount, not only their own share.
story:
The lease arrived as a PDF at 4:07 on a Thursday, and William opened it at his desk with the fan pushing warm air against his neck. Three names on page one: William, Edith, Ayan. Unit 4C, Ashland Street, twelve months, a rent figure that looked reasonable until he multiplied it by twelve. He scrolled past the photographs the landlord had attached, past the paragraph about noise, and stopped where the words grew dense.

"Each tenant shall be jointly and severally liable," he read aloud, then read it again, quieter, because the phrase refused to become plain no matter how slowly he moved his eyes across it. He was halfway through drafting a text to Edith when Ayan called, his voice already carrying the brightness of someone who had signed things before and found them uneventful.

"It's a standard lease," Ayan said. "My cousin signed one in Columbus. You just initial the margins and send it back."

"Jointly and severally liable," William said. "What does that actually mean?"

There was a pause long enough that William could hear Ayan's television in the background, someone scoring a goal in a stadium very far from Ashland Street. "It means we all owe it. Together."

William wasn't satisfied, and the dissatisfaction felt physical, a small stone under the tongue. He opened a second tab, then a third, sequestering the lease in one corner of the screen while he searched the phrase in another. He found a legal aid site with a plain-language page, and a forum where a woman described her experience in short, flat sentences. He read for eleven minutes without moving.

"Edith," he said when she picked up, because he had muted Ayan and dialed without deciding to. "Did you read the liability part?"

"I skimmed it. Why, what did you do?"

"Nothing. Listen. If one of us doesn't pay, the landlord can come after any of us for the whole thing. Not just our third. The entire rent. That's what joint and several liability means." He heard her exhale, the sound of a person sitting down somewhere without a chair having been offered.

"The whole rent," she repeated. "For all of us, or for you?"

"Any of us. Each one of us. They pick, or it works out that way, and you could owe everything."

"This is why my mom says never sign anything," Edith said, but her voice had lost its joke. In the background of her end, a door closed.

William brought Ayan back into a three-way call, and for twenty minutes the conversation ran in circles that felt almost tautological: they agreed they should only sign what they agreed to, and they agreed they couldn't agree until they understood what they were agreeing to. Ayan argued from experience, or from the borrowed experience of his cousin, whose landlord had been kind and whose water heater had never failed. Edith argued from her mother, from a childhood of contracts that had gone wrong in ways she described only partially. William found himself doing something stranger than either, holding both positions at once, saying "you're right" to Ayan and "you're also right" to Edith, and meaning both, and knowing that meaning both was not a position but a postponement of one.

"You two are going to be great at this," Ayan said eventually, not kindly and not unkindly. "Law school acumen. Meanwhile I need to give notice on my dorm room by Monday or I lose the deposit."

"That's the deposit," William said. "This is twelve months of rent."

"I know what it is."

Edith proposed a compromise: each of them could ask a parent to look at it over the weekend. Ayan said his father worked Saturdays and wouldn't read English legal text easily anyway. William looked at the signature page, at the three empty lines printed neatly with their names beneath, and thought about how a signature was supposed to be the simplest thing in the world, a person agreeing to what a document said, except that the document said more than any of them had understood an hour ago, and probably more than they understood now.

Then Edith laughed, a single short note, and said, "Wait. Look at page six. The guarantor line." William scrolled. Beneath each tenant's signature block there was a second line, smaller, labeled guarantor, and under the first of them, in blue ink, in handwriting that was not William's and not Ayan's, someone had already signed.

"Whose name is that under?" Ayan asked, though the formatting made it clear, and William zoomed in on the scan the landlord had sent, the version already returned once by someone, and read his own name sitting above a signature he had never made.

"That's mine," he said. "That line is mine."

His mother was downstairs making dinner; he could hear the exhaust fan and the clatter of a pan, and he thought of her signature on forms all his life, permission slips and field trips and emergency contacts, her name standing in for his because he had been small, and he understood in one cold drop that somewhere between then and now the rule had changed without anyone announcing it. He looked at the line again, at the ink that had no right to be there, and typed into the group chat: Nobody signs anything until we figure this out. Then, before he could soften it, before he could add a thumbs up or an exclamation mark to make it easier, he pressed send.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: In Java, a field marked private can be read or changed only by code inside the same class.
story:
The library on Delancey closed at nine, and by seven Charlotte had claimed the corner table by the window, her laptop open to a file named BankAccount.java that refused to behave. The assignment was due at midnight: build a class with private fields, write getter methods, write a test class, and get it running. She had told Kenzie at lunch that it would take an hour, tops, and Kenzie had said, "You always say that," and Charlotte had said, "And I'm always basically right," which was true often enough to be dangerous.

The class itself was written. She had a field called balance, marked private the way the slides showed, and a method called getBalance that returned it. That part had felt almost elegant, like sealing a letter. The trouble was the test. Her test file tried to read balance directly, and the compiler kept spitting back an error she didn't understand, something about balance having private access, and no matter how many times she reread her code the error stayed exactly the same.

Charles-Emile arrived at seven-forty with two hot chocolates and the untroubled posture of someone who had finished the assignment on Tuesday. He set a cup beside her keyboard and leaned over her screen without asking, which she both hated and needed.

"You're doing it wrong," he said.

"I know it's wrong. I don't know why."

He tapped the screen once, at the line where her test tried to touch balance. "Private," he said. "A field marked private can be read or changed only by code inside the same class."

Charlotte stared at the line. It was such a small rule, and it had eaten her whole evening. "So my test can't get in at all?"

"Not through the field. Through the getter."

Here was the thing she had not told anyone, the thing she had been amortizing across three weeks of nods and half-understood nods since the semester began: she had signed up for the intermediate section because the beginner one was full, and because her mother had said, "You're good at this, you'll catch up," and because Charlotte had wanted to believe her. Every assignment since had been a payment on a debt she'd taken on with herself, interest accruing quietly. Tonight the debt had come due all at once, and the visceral certainty that she was about to be found out sat in her stomach like a swallowed stone.

Charles-Emile was already pulling a chair over. He didn't ask why she'd written the test that way, which was a mercy, and also a small mystery, because a person who finished assignments on Tuesday should have found her mistake obvious and funny. Instead he said, "Delete that line. Call the getter instead. And your setter, does it validate anything?"

"It's supposed to reject negative deposits."

"Then your test should check that it does. That's the whole point of the wall." He said it without condescension, the way Mr. Delgado said things in the lab, and Charlotte remembered Mr. Delgado stopping at her row last week, pausing a moment too long, and how she'd hunched over her keyboard certain he could see the gap in her knowledge like a hole in a sweater.

She fixed the test. She wrote a second test, and a third, deliberately breaking each one before making it pass, because she'd read somewhere that a test you haven't seen fail proves nothing. The compiler's complaints shifted from accusations about access to plain arithmetic, which felt almost friendly. At eight-thirty Kenzie appeared at the table with a history textbook and no hot chocolate, having deduced from Charlotte's silence all evening that something was wrong.

"Did you finish?"

"It's running," Charlotte said. "All tests pass."

Kenzie waited, because Kenzie knew her. And Charlotte found that the sentence she'd been dreading was smaller than she'd imagined. "I've been behind since week one," she said. "The beginner section was full and I just pretended."

Charles-Emile shrugged, as if culpability were a currency he didn't accept. "Everyone starts somewhere private," he said, and grinned at his own joke, and Charlotte laughed before she'd decided to.

The screen glowed green, three tests passing, and through the window the streetlights were coming on along Delancey. She still wasn't sure she'd catch up, only that she wanted to, and she opened the syllabus to see what came next.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: English newspaper headlines often drop small words like 'the' and use the present tense for past events, a compressed style sometimes called 'headlinese'.
story:
The festival had spread itself across the whole park, and Amy had volunteered for the international news stand mostly because Dalia had batted her eyes and said please, and secondly because the stand promised free samosas for helpers. Ms. Kelly, who ran the stand, had one job for her: read a short article in English, the language Amy had been studying for two years, and summarise it aloud to visitors, every hour, on the little wooden stage. Two years of grammar books, and now she had to actually speak, in public, to strangers.

Her first attempt was a disaster of the gentlest kind. She stood at the podium with a folded newspaper, chose what looked like the shortest article, and got stuck on the title. "'Mayor Opens Bridge Collapses'?" she read slowly. "This is not a sentence. This is... words that have fallen off a shelf." A man in the front row laughed kindly. Three people wandered toward the dumpling stall. Dalia, sitting cross-legged at the edge of the stage eating a samosa, called out, "Maybe the bridge fell on the mayor?"

"No," Amy said, staring at the page. "Look, there is no 'the'. There is no 'has'. English has articles, I have suffered through them. Where did they go?" She flipped to another headline. "'Council Rejects Plan'. Also no 'the'. Also no 'did' or 'has'. It is like the newspaper is trying to save money on ink."

Ms. Kelly passed by carrying a crate of lemonade and paused. "You've found headlinese," she said, and kept walking.

Amy repeated the word to herself, mouthing it. Headlinese. So it had a name, which meant it was a thing, a style, not just her own failure. She sat down on the stage steps next to Dalia and took half the samosa without asking. "Okay. Think. The bridge did collapse. That already happened. But the headline says 'opens' and 'collapses' like it is happening right now. And the small words, the 'the', the 'is', they are just... gone."

"English is showing off," Dalia said. "Look how efficient I am, I do not need my auxiliary verbs, I am a language of business."

"That is actually it, though." Amy sat up straighter. "The little words are the auxiliary ones, the helpers, and the headlines throw them out. And they use the present tense even for things that already happened. So 'Mayor Opens Bridge' means the mayor opened a bridge. Last week, probably. It already happened, but they write it like now."
