She read the article under the headline and confirmed it: the mayor had opened the bridge on Tuesday, and on Wednesday a section of it had sagged, and now there was an inquiry. Two past events, compressed into six words with no grammar she recognised.

"Two years of English," she said, "and the newspapers have a secret dialect nobody teaches you."

"Maybe if you'd studied something useful instead, like philosophy, you would know an ontology when you see one."

"It is not an ontology, Dalia, it is a headline."

"It is a whole theory of what counts as a word. Apparently 'the' does not count. 'The' has been voted off the island."

Amy laughed, then went quiet, because the next summary slot was in ten minutes and she had to decide something. She could translate the headline into full, careful sentences, grammar restored, every "the" lovingly returned, and sound like a textbook. Or she could keep the compression and explain it, hold both ways of thinking at once: the English that drops things and the English that keeps them. But she was still not sure she had it right. Maybe some headlines kept their small words. Maybe the present tense did not always mean the past. She only had this one paper and one hour, and the honest thing was to say so out loud.

When the small crowd gathered again, she held up the newspaper. "The headline says 'Mayor Opens Bridge Collapses'. I want to tell you what I learned today. Headlines in English drop small words like 'the', and they use the present tense even for events that already happened. So this is not happening now, and it is not a bridge falling on a mayor. It is a bridge that opened and then partly failed." She summarised the rest of the article, slowly, and a woman in the front nodded and said she finally understood why English news had always looked broken to her.

Afterward Dalia stood, dusted crumbs off her knees, and held out the last samosa, split unevenly, the bigger half toward Amy. Amy took the bigger half anyway. "So," Dalia said, "tomorrow, headlines. Next week, poetry."

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: An argument from silence draws a conclusion from what a source fails to mention; historians treat it with caution because writers record only what seems important to them.
story:
The monument stood where the road bent away from the river, a slab of grey metamorphic rock polished on one face and rough on the other, cut from a quarry forty miles north and hauled down before anyone alive could remember. Kaylee had walked past it all her life. Today she stood in front of it with a notebook, because Ms. Ong had assigned each of them a local landmark and a question about it, and Kaylee's question had come to her the night her grandfather laughed.

She had been at his kitchen table in March, reading aloud from a project about the 1919 influenza, and she had said, "The parade must not have happened, because your diary from that fall never mentions it." He laughed so hard he had to set down his coffee. "Girl, I wrote two lines a week. Weather and prices. You can't hang a conclusion on what I left out." He tapped the little green book. "People only write down what matters to them that day. The rest of the world just walks on by." She had felt stupid, and then curious, and the feeling had never quite left.

Willyam arrived on his bike, skidding gravel, with Frank trailing behind eating something out of foil. "You found it yet?" Willyam asked. His project shared hers, because Ms. Ong had paired them deliberately, and for three weeks they had been arguing about the mill strike of 1911, when, according to Kaylee's great-grandmother's stories, forty women walked out of the Alcott mill and shut it down for eleven days. According to Willyam, it never happened.

"The town ledger is the official record," he said now, pacing the monument's base. "It's meticulous. Council minutes, tax rolls, everything. And it says nothing about a strike. No closure, no dispute, nothing. If forty women had walked out, the town would have written it down."

"An argument from silence," Kaylee said. It was a phrase she had worked out at her grandfather's table, turning over what he'd told her, and she said it now the way you'd set a stone on a wall. "You're drawing a conclusion from what a source fails to mention. Grandpa says historians treat it with real caution, because writers only record what seems important to them." She watched his face to see whether it landed.

Frank, who had no stake in the project and therefore the clearest head of the three, pointed his foil at the polished face of the monument. "Then what's this thing about?" he said. "It says the town was built by industry and the vision of its founders." The three of them read the dedication together, chiselled in a seriffed font, nineteen names incised below it. Kaylee had never counted the names before. Nineteen men, every one of them an owner, a banker, a mayor. No one who had spun thread.

"That proves my point," Willyam said, quieter than before. "The town made this. The town made the ledger. Same silence twice." But Kaylee was already kneeling at the rough back face of the stone, where lichen had colonised the unpolished gneiss, and where, half a metre above the soil line, someone had scratched letters with something harder than a knife. The strokes were shallow and amateur. It took her a long moment to read W-E-S-T-G-A-T-E, and then, below it, a date: 1911.

"My great-grandmother's name was Westgate," she said. Her voice came out strange, and she let it. "She said the women gathered here before the walkout. There wasn't a monument then, just the quarry stone they hadn't hauled off yet. She said they stood on it so the mill office could see them over the fence line." She put her palm flat against the scratched letters. The rock was cold even in the sun.

They stood around it for a while without anyone trying to claim it. Willyam crouched beside her, took out his phone, and photographed the letters at an angle so the raking light would catch them. "If it's really her handwriting, it's a source," he admitted. "A weird one. Graffiti on a rock." He looked up at Kaylee, and something in his expression had shifted, though not surrendered. "But it doesn't tell us the strike worked, or how long it lasted, or whether the ledger men left it out on purpose or just didn't think forty women were worth ink. I still want to know that."

"Me too," Kaylee said. "That's the part I can't get to. We know the silence is real. We don't know why it's silent." She copied the date into her notebook, then, on impulse, the nineteen founders' names as well, because a list of who got remembered was itself a kind of record. Ms. Ong was due to meet them at the monument at noon, and when she came down the path with her coffee, Kaylee and Willyam were still crouched behind the stone like conspirators, arguing over whether a scratched name counted as testimony or as a boast.

Ms. Ong peered at the letters, and then at the polished face with its nineteen names, and back again, and said nothing for a full ten seconds. "Well," she said. "The town spent good money on that front face. Nobody ever paid a cent for this one." She took a long drink of her coffee and looked out at the river. "I wonder which one the school board had in mind when it approved your project topics."

Frank folded his foil into a neat square and said, "The one that fits on the plaque."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Java was released by Sun Microsystems in 1995; its lead designer was James Gosling.
story:
The laptop Aaliyah's brother had left in the basement was moribund in the way of machines that have outlived their owners' interest, and it took four minutes to boot, so Zoe spent those minutes rereading the assignment sheet. Build a class in Java, it said, with private fields and getter methods, then test it. She understood the words individually. Together they formed a sentence she could not picture, which was the feeling she had learned to treat as the start of something rather than the end.

Aaliyah came down the stairs carrying two mugs and a bag of pretzels, her phone wedged against her shoulder. "Ayana says she'll come after her shift," she said, dropping the phone on the couch. "She also says you're overthinking, and that a class is just a container." Zoe pulled the laptop toward her and opened the editor. "A container with locks on it," she said. "That's what private means, I think. The fields are private, so nobody outside can touch them, and then the getter methods are like the little windows you hand things through."

She typed the first line, Book, and then the fields, title and pages, both marked private, and the compiler accepted them without complaint, which felt like a small act of grace. The getter methods came next, public String getTitle, return title, and she sat back. "But why?" she said. "If I'm the one writing both parts, why would I lock my own fields away from myself?" Aaliyah, who was spreading pretzels into a fan shape on the table, said that sounded like a question Zoe would ask, and that most people would just do the assignment.

Zoe's mother studied immune responses for a living, and all through Zoe's childhood dinner had been a place where the word antigen drifted through, something the body recognizes and reacts to, foreign and requiring an answer. She noticed, sitting there in the lamplight of the basement, that her mind had offered her the comparison on its own: the private fields were somehow like that, marked as self, and anything outside was other, and the getters were the controlled channel between them. She didn't say it aloud, because Aaliyah was already halfway into a story about the robotics competition last spring, and Zoe let her talk.

"Remember when that senior argued with the judge about the code being ancient?" Aaliyah said. "He was shocked. He kept saying, it came out in 1995, and the judge had to tell him the lead designer was this guy, James Gosling, at Sun Microsystems. He couldn't get over that the language was older than he was." Zoe laughed. "Older than us too." Something about this pleased her and she couldn't have said exactly why, except that a thing could be old and still be the thing you were learning at eleven at night in a basement, that the locks she was building had been designed by a person with a name, in a year she could count backward from.

Ayana arrived with her work polo still on and her hair smelling like the café, and she planted herself on the couch arm. "Pontificate for me," she said. "Aaliyah says you've been philosophizing about privacy." Zoe turned the laptop so they could see the screen. "It's not philosophy, it's a rule, and I can't decide if the rule is protection or just ceremony. If my test class calls getTitle, it gets the title. If it tries to touch the title directly, the compiler stops it. So the field is safe, but safe from whom? From me." Ayana considered this while eating a pretzel. "From the you who isn't paying attention," she said.

That landed somewhere real, and Zoe wrote the test next, a main method that made a Book, printed what the getter returned, and ran it. The output appeared exactly as expected, the title and the page count sitting in the black window like facts that had been true all along and had merely been waiting to be asked politely. She changed one field's value in the test, ran it again, and watched the getter return the new value, and she understood, finally, the shape of the thing: you built the walls and the windows in the same act, and the walls made the windows mean something.

Still, the question Ayana had half-answered stayed open in her, the way questions that matter tend to. Whether the discipline was in the language or in the programmer, whether a rule you set for yourself counted as freedom or its opposite. She closed the editor, saved, and looked at the two of them. "Again tomorrow?" Aaliyah said, already stacking the mugs. "Same basement, same moribund laptop?" Zoe pulled the power cord out and wound it around her hand. "Bring pretzels," she said. "And maybe the one with the salt."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The number of moles in a sample equals its mass in grams divided by its molar mass in grams per mole.
story:
The garage smelled of yeast and motor oil, because Vienna's family used it for both. Half held her father's dormant motorcycle, shrouded in a tarp, and the other half held a steel table, a scaled-down oven, and stacked tins of flour that had to last until Friday's market. Carter sat on an overturned milk crate with his chemistry notebook open on his knee, and the quiz from Thursday lay beside him with its red slash across the top like a wound.

"Sixty percent," he said. "She wrote it twice."

"Ms. Leblanc writes it twice when she thinks you're not trying," Vienna said, weighing flour into a bowl on a small digital scale. She did not look up. "When you're trying and failing, she writes it once."

He considered which was worse. The second problem on the quiz had asked how many moles of a product you would get from a given mass of reactant, and Carter had multiplied where he should have divided, or divided where he should have multiplied, and the answer had come out absurd, a number so large it should have embarrassed him. He had written it anyway and turned the page in, an act of quiet surrender he could still feel in his wrist.

"How much flour is that?" he asked, to change the subject.

"Twelve hundred grams for the big batch, three hundred for the small." She leveled the scale with the edge of a knife, an ascetic little gesture, exact and unhurried, nothing wasted. "My dad says you don't learn bread by cups. Cups lie. Grams don't."

Carter watched the numbers on the scale climb and settle. Three hundred grams. Twelve hundred. Four small batches to one big. He turned back to his notebook, where he had copied the problem again in ink that morning: given so many grams of a reactant, find the moles. He had been staring at it in his bedroom for an hour last night, circling the word molar mass as if circling it would make it confess.

"You know what a mole is?" he asked.

"In chemistry? It's a number of particles," Vienna said. "A specific number. Ms. Leblanc made us memorize it sophomore year." She tipped the flour into the bowl and brushed the scale clean with her palm.

He looked at the empty scale. Zero grams, waiting. Then at his problem, where the reactant had a mass in grams and the substance had a molar mass in grams per mole, a number printed in the table at the back of the book like a fact about a person's character. Flour did not have a character exactly, but it had a weight per batch, a fixed ratio, and if you knew the weight and the ratio you knew the batch. He tried it the way Vienna would: mass divided by the weight per unit.

"Wait," he said. He turned the notebook flat on the steel table, in the drift of flour dust. "The grams of the reactant, divided by grams per mole. That gives moles." He said it slowly, the way you test a plank before stepping on it. "The number of moles equals the mass in grams divided by the molar mass in grams per mole." His pencil found the division sign and the numbers fell through it, one into the other, and the answer came out small and reasonable, a quantity you could hold.

"That's how you doubled the recipe last month," Vienna said, glancing over. "You just didn't know you were doing math."

"It's not the same thing."

"It's the same shape of thing."

He wanted to argue and found he could not. His father kept a taxonomy of worth in the garage at home, a private sorting of work that counted and work that did not, and schoolwork sat near the top while baking and motorcycles and anything done with hands sat near the bottom. Carter had inherited the categories without ever examining them. It occurred to him now that dividing grams by grams per mole in a garage beside an oven was the same act as doing it under a fluorescent light in Room 214, and that neither location could predicate whether the thinking was real.

What he could not decide, and did not try to settle in that moment, was whether he had failed the quiz because the idea was hard or because he had refused to let it be familiar. He remembered choosing to stop working at minute eleven of the period, remembered the specific comfort of giving up, and he weighed it now the way Vienna weighed flour, without excuse, letting it sit on the scale.

He copied the corrected problem into the back of his notebook, every step, then did the next two from the book. The second one he got wrong, checked it, and found he had used the molar mass of the wrong substance, a smaller and more honest error. Vienna pulled the first loaf from the oven and set it on the rack to cool, and its heat reached the milk crate where Carter sat, still writing, his pencil down to a stub. When she thumped the loaf's bottom with two knuckles and held it out to him, he took it with the hand not holding the pencil and tore off the heel.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: An off-book rehearsal is one where actors must perform without their scripts, having memorised their lines.
story:
Mason had claimed the living room for three weeks straight, and his mother had stopped asking when the furniture would return to its original arrangement. The coffee table stood against the wall, the couch had become "the audience," and blue painter's tape marked the edges of an imaginary stage between the TV and the bay window. He walked the space alone before anyone arrived, holding the script of the one-act open in both hands like a map of a country he had never visited, and he made a small pencil mark where Anastasia would cross, and another where Heath would not.

The play was fifteen minutes long, a two-hander about siblings dividing their dead father's tools, and Mr. Shevchenko, who ran the drama program, had given Mason the directing job with a warning: the whole thing rises or falls on whether you get them to move like people, not chess pieces. Mason had nodded as though he understood. He did not yet understand. He had spent the first rehearsal positioning Anastasia and Heath like furniture, moving them by the elbow, and Anastasia had finally said, gently, "You're placing us. Let us find it." So tonight, the third rehearsal, he intended to say less. He had read somewhere that the director's vision had to be strong enough to bend without breaking, strong enough to hold other people's instincts without subsuming them, though he suspected he had it backwards half the time.

Heath arrived twenty minutes late with his script still unread, its pages fanning open to show clean, unmarked margins. Anastasia arrived on time with hers bristling with highlights, tabs, marginal questions in three colors. "I set a date," Mason said, before either of them sat down. "Next Thursday. Off-book." Heath looked at the ceiling. "Which means what, exactly?" "No scripts in hand," Mason said. "Lines memorised. You perform without the pages." Heath nodded slowly, the nod of a man agreeing to something he had already decided to fail at, and Anastasia said, "Good. I'll be ready," with a flatness that made it a challenge rather than a promise.

They ran the first scene, and it went badly in an instructive way. Heath, holding his script like a shield, could not gesture, could not cross the taped line, could not pick up the prop wrench when the moment came because his hands were full of paper. Anastasia kept adjusting her own blocking to rescue him, drifting upstage to receive his lines instead of holding her mark, and Mason watched his careful pencil diagram dissolve into something improvised and, he had to admit, more alive in patches. He called a halt. "Heath, put the script on the couch. Just for this run. If you dry, I'll prompt." "I'll dry immediately," Heath said. "Then we'll find out what happens after you dry," Mason said, and Heath set the pages down as though surrendering a hostage.

Anastasia read her lines with the script abandoned from the first beat, and something changed in the room. She paused where pausing was right. She picked up the wrench. She said the line about the father's hands, which Mason had privately considered sentimental, and it landed. Heath dried four times, and each time Mason prompted from the couch without standing, and each time Heath found the line and then, once, found something extra in it, a bitterness Mason had not imagined. Later, after they'd gone, Heath texted him, and Mason sat on the arm of the couch reading it under the lamp.

"I'm not going to be off-book by Thursday," the message said. "You know that, right? I got cast because nobody else would take the part. I got cast because I owe Shevchenko a favor from the robotics thing. I'm the disaffected guy who does the jobs nobody wants." Mason typed and deleted three replies. "You were better tonight without the script," he finally sent. "The one dry, where you got angry, that was the best thing you've done." The reply came back: "That was me being actually angry, not acting." Mason stared at the screen. He typed, "Then use it," and after that Heath's icon went quiet, and the room held only the lamp hum and the tape lines glowing faintly on the hardwood.

At school the next day, Mr. Shevchenko caught him in the corridor and asked how it was going, and Mason said the thing he'd been assembling all morning: that he'd started out thinking a director's job was control, drawing the arrows, deciding where everyone stood, and he'd started to think it was closer to what Anastasia did with her highlights, marking what mattered and letting the rest be discovered. "But I can't tell," he said, "if that's real or if it's just me covering for the fact that Heath hasn't learned his lines." Mr. Shevchenko laughed, which was not helpful, and said only, "Both things can be true," and walked off toward the gym, leaving Mason with a sentence he would turn over for days.

Thursday came. Anastasia stood on her mark with her hands empty and her eyes ready. Heath came in from the kitchen holding his script, and Mason said nothing, and Heath stood at the taped line for a long moment, looking at the pages, then folded them in half and put them in his back pocket. He dried twice in the first scene, and both times Anastasia covered the gap without changing her feet, and once Heath reached into the pocket as if for a lifeline and touched the folded paper through the denim and left it there. They finished the run. Nobody applauded, because there was nobody to applaud, just the couch and the lamp and the blue tape, and when it was over Anastasia asked, "Same time Sunday?" and Mason, still holding his own marked-up script that he no longer knew what to do with, said, "Yeah. Sunday."

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Simon Schama's Citizens, published in 1989 for the Revolution's bicentenary, argued that violence was an essential part of the Revolution from 1789 onward.
story:
The bus from the college had dropped them at the gates of the old estate with instructions to gather in the orangery by noon, and Peyton, who had wanted to sit alone, found herself walking the gravel path beside Alexe and Elie anyway. Ms. Henry had assigned the historiographical essay before they left: how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800, which meant they were supposed to care not about the Revolution itself but about the arguments people had had about it for two hundred years. Peyton had a notebook and a dull pencil and the uneasy sense that everyone else had already chosen a side.

They had come to the estate because its library held a shelf of Revolution histories, first editions and cheap reprints alike, gathered by some dour Victorian whose portrait frowned above the fireplace. Ms. Henry wanted them to hold the books, she said, to see how the arguments took physical shape across the decades. Alexe, who read fast and talked faster, had already found an 1847 copy of Carlyle and was holding it at arm's length like something that might bite.

"The Terror was a detour," Alexe said, turning the book over. "The Revolution starts with liberty and ends with the guillotine because everything went wrong in between. That's the story people told for ages. Things bent off course."

Elie, sitting cross-legged on the floor between the stacks, looked up. "You're about forty years behind, then. Schama said the opposite." Peyton watched Elie pull a fat paperback out of her bag, its cover softened from being carried around. "Citizens. It came out in 1989, for the bicentenary. He argued that violence wasn't a detour at all. It was essential to the Revolution from 1789 onward, right from the start."

Alexe remonstrated, saying that couldn't be right, that everyone knew the Terror came later, in 1793, and that a revolution about rights could not have been born killing. Elie only tapped the paperback's cover and said the book was eight hundred pages and she'd read most of them, and that Schama hadn't said the killing started in 1789, only that it was woven in from the beginning, part of the thing itself. Peyton wrote the title in her notebook, underlined it twice, and felt the ground under her own half-formed opinion shift.

She had come to the essay believing what Alexe believed, mostly because the belief was tidy. In her draft, which she'd started on the bus, the Revolution had a clean arc, rising toward promise and then falling, like a piece of music that builds and breaks. She remembered, with a small sting, the moment in tenth grade when she'd argued the same thing in class so stubbornly that a boy in the back row had finally said, "You just like tidy endings," and she hadn't spoken to him for a week. Now she sat in a room full of dead men's books and wondered whether tidiness was a way of thinking or just a way of not thinking.

"Show me the part," Alexe said, less certain now, and Elie flipped pages and read aloud a passage about crowds and blood, and then another, her voice dropping as though the room demanded a diminuendo, until the sentences came out nearly in a whisper. Around them the other students drifted between shelves. Ms. Henry passed once, paused, said nothing, and moved on, which Peyton understood as permission.

"Maybe they're both half right," Peyton said, before she had decided to say anything. Both girls looked at her. "I mean, the essay isn't asking which one is true. It's asking how the view changed. Carlyle in 1847 sees a tragedy of excess. Schama in 1989, on the bicentenary, sees violence as essential from the start. Something happened between those two books to change the question."

"Like what?" Alexe asked.

"I don't know yet. That's the part I can't find here." Peyton turned her pencil over in her fingers. "I'm honest about that. I know the view shifted and I know Schama's claim, and I don't yet know everything that shifted it. Maybe the essay can say that. Maybe it's allowed to say that."

At noon they gathered in the orangery, glass overhead, light coming down green and milky through the panes. Ms. Henry asked each of them for one sentence about what they'd found. Alexe, to Peyton's surprise, said, "I changed my mind about something," and then, when Ms. Henry waited, added only, "Ask Peyton." Peyton opened her notebook to the underlined title, and the words she had written beneath it, which were not an answer but a question, and she read them out loud: "Was the Terror a detour, or was it built in from the beginning?" Ms. Henry looked at the page, then at the three of them, and said, "Now go find out."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type, not even void.
story:
The computer lab smelled of warm monitors and the custodian's lemon cleaner, and Madison had been staring at the same twenty lines of code for eleven minutes. The assignment on Ms. Joseph's whiteboard read, in blue marker that had gone pale: Build a Book class with private fields, a constructor, and getter methods. Test it in a runner class. Madison had the fields done, three of them, private String title, private String author, private int pages, each one tidy behind its keyword like a secret in a drawer. Her friend Vanessa leaned across the aisle, chewing the cap of a pen.

"Yours compiles?" Vanessa asked.

"Everything except the test," Madison said. "The runner makes a Book, but when I print the title it comes out null."

"Null." Vanessa said the word the way you'd say the name of a disease. She wheeled her chair over without waiting for an invitation, and her sleeve knocked the mouse so the screensaver of Reece's machine two rows back woke up. Reece, who had finished early and been pretending to play a typing game for half an hour, drifted over too, hands in his hoodie pocket.

Madison scrolled to the top of her file. There it was, the method she'd written to set up the object's starting values: public void Book(String t, String a, int p). It looked right to her. It had the name of the class, the parentheses, the assignments inside. She had even run it in her head, line by line, the way Ms. Joseph had taught them, and in her head it worked fine. In the actual machine, the title stayed null, the pages stayed zero, as if the method had simply declined to exist.

"I wrote the setup method," Madison said. "It assigns everything. It just doesn't run."

Reece put one finger on the screen, touching the word void. "Why'd you put that there?"

"Because methods have return types. Ms. Joseph said every method needs one." Even as she said it, the sentence felt wrong in her mouth, too wide, like a borrowed coat. Not every method. Something in her resisted the generalization, and she stared at the line until her eyes watered, half furious at the compiler and half furious at herself.

Then Vanessa saw it, and I watched her see it, because I'd been watching Madison's face go through its whole weather system for the better part of ten minutes. Vanessa wasn't smarter than Madison, whatever the gradebook implied; she was just faster at admitting when a rule she'd memorized didn't fit the case in front of her. She reached past Madison's wrist and deleted the word void, five letters gone with four keystrokes, and sat back with her arms crossed like she'd disarmed something.

"There," Vanessa said. "Run it."

Madison ran it. The console filled with clean black text, the title printing exactly as typed, the pages printing 312, and the feeling that went through her was visceral, a shock low in the stomach, because nothing had changed except five deleted letters and yet the whole program had come alive. "A Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type," she said slowly, reading the fact off the deleted line the way you'd read a footprint off a floor. "Not even void."

"So it's not a method," Reece said.

"I don't know what it is." Madison said it flatly, and she didn't soften it. She copied the corrected line onto the corner of her handout in small letters, then, beneath it, wrote why? and left the why unanswered, because the compiler didn't owe her reasons tonight and Ms. Joseph wasn't at her elbow. Ms. Joseph was at her desk across the lab, red pen moving through a stack of quizzes, and Madison raised her hand anyway, then lowered it halfway, then raised it again.

When Ms. Joseph came over, Madison turned the monitor toward her and pointed at the runner's output instead of the code. "It works now," she said. "I want to know why void breaks it. Not the rule. The reason."

Ms. Joseph looked at the screen, then at Madison, and did that thing she did where she smiled without giving anything away. "Put that question at the top of your test file as a comment," she said. "Bring it Thursday. I want you to try answering it yourself first."

Behind them the bell rang, shrill through the hallway speakers, and half the lab began logging off. Madison didn't move. She was retyping the why? comment at the top of her file, cursor blinking after the question mark, and Vanessa stood in the doorway with her bag on one shoulder, waiting to see if Madison would come.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: In We Now Know, published in 1997 after Soviet archives had partly opened, Gaddis placed much more responsibility on Stalin personally for the Cold War.
story:
Nicolas spread the two books on the kitchen table the way other people laid out cards. The first was the library's battered copy of Gaddis's earlier volume, checked out three times already this semester, and the second was We Now Know, published in 1997, which Ms. Pereira had pressed on him after class with the words "you'll want to see what changed." He had assumed she meant the writing. It took him forty minutes at the table, a cooling mug of tea beside him, to understand she meant the argument itself: the same historian, the same war, and a different verdict. In the earlier book the Cold War read as a kind of deadlock, two systems locked in a structure neither could escape. In the later one, Stalin's own character carried the weight. Nicolas wrote in the margin of his notebook, "same man, new archives, new answer?" and underlined the question mark twice.

The essay prompt was simple and, for that reason, merciless: which explanation does the evidence better support, and why? Ms. Pereira had banned the word "balanced" in conclusions. "Balanced is where thinking goes to hide," she'd said, and Nicolas had laughed with everyone else and then spent a week discovering she was right.

His mother passed through the kitchen twice, wiping counters that were already clean. The second time she stopped behind his chair and read over his shoulder. "When I was your age we did the same war," she said. "It was going to be the end of everything, one winter or another." She set a plate of bread and cheese at his elbow without being asked. "It didn't end. That's what I know."

He worked until the window went dark, then texted Daniel, who lived two streets over and who understood the assignment in a way no one else in the class did, because Daniel had actually read both books the previous spring, before dropping the course to take extra shifts. Daniel replied that he'd come by, and Nicolas pushed the books to one end of the table to make room.

It was Nicolas's mother who opened the door, and she saw at once that something was wrong, though Daniel said nothing about it. He came in with his jacket still buttoned, which he never did, and he looked at the kitchen table like a man checking whether a bridge would hold him. She offered food; he refused; she poured him tea anyway and set it down and left them to it, deciding in the hallway that whatever it was, Nicolas would learn it or he wouldn't, and that a boy of eighteen sometimes needed to be the one to ask.

Daniel sat, picked up We Now Know, and turned it over in his hands. "So you found out," he said.

"Found out what?"

"That he changed his mind." Daniel tapped the cover. "Everyone treats it like a scandal. One of the TAs called it disloyal to his own book." He said it lightly, but he was watching Nicolas's face with an attention that had nothing to do with historiography. When Nicolas started to answer, Daniel added, "I deferred, by the way. A year. Money." He said "money" the way someone says a word they've rehearsed until it sounds casual.

Nicolas let that sit for a second, then slid the earlier volume across the table. "Then you have time to help me. Seriously. He wrote this one first, when all we had was what you could see from outside. Then the Soviet archives opened, partly, and he wrote We Know Now. And it's not that he abandoned everything. It's that the documents let him see a person where before he'd only seen a system. Stalin personally. He puts much more of it on Stalin personally." He heard himself speeding up and slowed down. "The question I can't get past is whether the new explanation is better because the evidence is better, or because blaming one man is just more satisfying than blaming a structure. Causality is the whole problem. A system can't sign documents. A dictator can."

"Or," Daniel said, "the old book had ossified into what everybody wanted to believe, and the archives cracked it." He was half smiling, but his fingers were tight around the mug. "You get to write about that. I get to install cable with Youcef's uncle."

"You could read the drafts," Nicolas said. "I mean it. You'd catch things I won't."

Daniel looked at the two books lying open side by side, the early one and the late one, the same war described by the same mind at twenty years' distance, and something in his shoulders loosened slightly. He unbuttoned his jacket. "Fine. But I'm not being polite about your topic sentences. And you're not allowed to end with 'more research is needed.'"

"That's literally what I was going to end with."

"Then we start there," Daniel said, and pulled his chair closer to the table.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Under US law, an artwork is protected by copyright automatically the moment it is created in a fixed form; registration is voluntary, though needed before suing over a US work.
story:
The poster in the art shed said BUILD YOUR PORTFOLIO: TEN PIECES, ONE THEME, ONE STATEMENT, and beneath it Ms. Hughes had written "Due Friday," which I chose to interpret as a suggestion. I am not, whatever Jayda says, a procrastinator. I am a person who believes inspiration cannot be scheduled, which is a philosophy, and philosophies take time, and by Wednesday I had one painting of a lake and a theme I described to anyone who asked as "water, broadly."

Tatiana had nine pieces by Wednesday. She was doing doors, all kinds, screen doors and shower doors and the door of the canoe shed, rendered in graphite so precise it looked like the doors might swing open. She had also, apparently, done research, which I found unfair, since the whole appeal of art was supposed to be that it came from somewhere unaccountable.

"Did you know," Tatiana said, spreading her doors across the picnic table like a card trick, "that the second you make something, like the actual second it's fixed, it's copyrighted? Automatically. You don't have to do anything."

"Then why does everyone watermark everything," I said, because I had a theory and the theory was that Tatiana made things up. She once told us the lake had a thermocline, which turned out to be true, which was annoying in a way I still hadn't forgiven.

Jayda was on her third attempt at a lanyard, which she had no intention of finishing. "My cousin got her stuff stolen off a website," she said. "Someone printed her drawing on shirts. She couldn't do anything about it."

"That's different," Tatiana said. "Here, the protection is automatic the moment the work exists in a fixed form. But if you want to sue somebody over a US work, you have to register it first. Registration's voluntary. It's just the thing you need before you can sue."

I said something like "fascinating" and went back to my lake, but I want to be honest, since honesty is allegedly my theme now, or second theme, or co-theme: I mostly heard the part about fixed form and thought about how nothing of mine was fixed anywhere except the walls of the art shed. That seemed significant. I decided it was significant. I had decided a lot of things that week.

Thursday evening I photographed the lake painting and, in a fit of something I called strategy, posted it with a watermark the size of a small country. Then I did a second piece, the lake at dusk, and a third, the lake reflected in a spoon, and by midnight I had three and a half paintings of water and a growing suspicion that "water, broadly" might be ossifying, if a theme can ossify, which Tatiana said it couldn't, because only living tissue could, but I meant it as a metaphor and I stand by the metaphor. A bad theme hardens exactly like that. You keep adding water pictures because the theme says water, and then the theme says nothing, and you have ten illustrations of a word.

I found Ms. Hughes at breakfast, drinking coffee like it was a legal obligation. I told her, and this is where I have to admit I presented it as my own insight, that I was thinking about the line between what an artist makes and what the world takes, and about how a thing is protected the instant it's fixed but the protection only becomes actionable through voluntary registration, and how maybe my theme should be about that, thresholds, the moment something becomes yours.

Ms. Hughes set down her coffee. "Tatiana told you about copyright."

I said that Tatiana had mentioned certain facts and that I had built upon them, which is how all art works anyway. Every artist is downstream of somebody, and there's no shame in a lineage, only in pretending you dug the river. She looked at me for a long moment, the look I would call sagacious if I wanted her to seem wiser than she was, and then she said, "Ten pieces. One theme. You have a day."

So here is what I made, or most of it. I took down the water paintings and painted thresholds instead: the doorway of the art shed with the light coming through, the exact edge of the dock where lake became not-lake, the spoon again, reframed, the moment before Tatiana's pencil touched paper, captured in a quick study of her hand that I did without asking and which I own now, automatically, the instant the graphite fixed it to the page, though I would register that one before suing her, if it came to that. The statement I wrote at 2 a.m. said that a thing becomes yours the moment it exists and takes the rest of your life to defend. Jayda read it over my shoulder and said, "Deep," in a tone I chose not to analyze.

Friday morning the portfolios went up on the clothesline Ms. Hughes had strung between two pines. My thresholds hung in a row, still slightly tacky, and Tatiana's doors hung opposite, and between them, when the wind lifted both sets at once, the doors and the thresholds almost touched. Ms. Hughes went down the line with her clipboard, and when she reached mine she stopped longer than she had stopped at anyone else's, which I took as a good sign, or decided to take as a good sign, which at this point is the same thing.

"You're missing one," she said finally, counting. "Nine."

I counted them myself, twice, and she was right, and there behind me, drying on the easel where I had abandoned it Wednesday night, was the lake painting, the first one, the one I had meant to throw away. I carried it over and held it up to the empty clip at the end of the line. The watermark covered half the water.

"That one's protected," Tatiana said from the next tree, not looking up. "The moment it's fixed."

"It was always fixed," I said, and clipped it on.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: On a stage in the round, the audience sits on all sides, so the director must keep actors moving so no section only sees their backs.
story:
The first rehearsal had gone badly, and Grace knew it before anyone said so. She had blocked the whole one-act as if the audience sat in one place, facing forward like a television, and the actors had walked their neat triangles while she nodded along. Then Ms. Berg had come to the dining room door with a mug of tea and mentioned that the performance had been moved, that chairs would now surround the playing space on every side, and that the room they were rehearsing in would be rearranged tomorrow to match. "You'll want to rethink your staging," was all she said, and Grace spent that night at the kitchen table with graph paper, drawing circles.

"We look like chess pieces," Josh said the next afternoon, when Grace had pushed the furniture to the walls and set the kitchen chairs in a ring. He had wanted the lead since auditions, had said so twice, and now he stood at the centre of the ring with his arms crossed, waiting. "From where I am, all I see is Lyra's back."

"That's the problem," Grace said. She walked the circle once, slowly, looking inward from each section of chairs. "Every side is somebody's front row."

Lyra, who had a habit of absconding with the good snacks before rehearsal even started, sat cross-legged in one of the chairs with a bag of pretzels and her script rolled in her hand. She was the only one who had read the play three times, and she had opinions about it, pithy ones, delivered like small verdicts. "He never stops moving in the text," she said. "Look at the stage directions. He's always leaving a room, coming back, crossing to the window. The play already wants to circle."

Grace stopped. She had been so pleased with her triangles, with the clean sightlines she had imagined, that she had ignored what the words were doing. She opened her script and read the directions again, and there it was, the traffic she had flattened into stillness. On a stage in the round, the audience sat on all sides, and the director had to keep the actors moving so no section only saw their backs. She had it backwards, she realized. She had been trying to hold people still for a single viewer, when the whole job now was motion.

"New plan," she said. "We spiral. Every time you two have a long exchange, you drift, slow, clockwise, and you counter-clockwise, so the backs keep trading sides." She demonstrated, walking the ring herself, and Josh watched with his head tilted.

"It'll look like we're fencing," he said, but he uncrossed his arms.

They ran the first scene four times. On the third try, Josh's drift turned into a real pivot, and he delivered his confession line while turning, so it swept the ring like a lighthouse, and Lyra answered him from the floor, having folded down into a crouch without being told. It was better than anything Grace had drawn on graph paper. It was also, she had to admit, not entirely hers. She had given them a principle, keep moving, trade the backs, and they had found the shape inside it, and she could not cleanly say where her directing ended and their instincts began. She decided she could live without knowing.

"Where'd you learn that thing about the backs?" Lyra asked afterward, gathering chairs while Josh, who had not been given the ending he wanted for his character, argued gently for a rewrite he was not going to get. Grace was stacking the graph paper, the circles and triangles, both sets now, into her folder.

"I figured it out standing where you're standing," she said. "Every chair is somebody's front row." Then, quieter, to herself, she counted the sections of the ring and chose where to sit for the next rehearsal, the one side she had never yet watched from.

"Places from the top," she called, and clapped twice.
